subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, April 24th, the debate on the motion of Hon. J. A. Robb (Acting Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the House to go into committee of Ways and Means and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Woodsworth.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
On rising, Mr. Speaker, to take part in the discussion on the budget, I wish to state that I broach the subject entirely devoid of any party feeling; the circumstances are too grave, the conditions of the country are too serious to mix up with politics; I, therefore, think it is the duty of all members of this House to frankly and freely express their opinion.
First, let me congratulate the government on behalf of the electors that I have the honour to represent here for having taken off the duty on a great number of items, among others on farming implements, and, for having found it possible to reduce the taxes. I was under the impression that such an announcement would cause joy throughout the country. I was further under the impression that the Conservatives could hardly criticize this measure, but I had not taken into account their inconsistency. Indeed, Sir, I recall that, during the session of 1922, the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) moved an amendment to the budget, seconded by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), reproaching the government for hot keeping their pledges: "The Liberal party"- they state-"at their great convention, in 1919, had promised should they be returned to power, to remove the duty on farming implements and they are not doing so, they are not fulfilling their pledges; therefore, they do not deserve the confidence of the people." To-day, after a lapse of hardly two years, these same gentlemen taunt the government for living up to their promises by removing the duty on farming implements. Is it possible to be so devoid of sincerity? Can one imagine anything more inconsistent? I do not think so. Let the government take no notice of their critics, let them follow up,

The Budget-Mr. Fontaine
without fear, this national policy that they have just inaugaurated; it is more than time to have this conflict existing between the East and West cease; the time is ripe to put an end to that class politics which has existed throughout the country for some years past by rendering justice to all classes of society. If we want this country to expand, confederation to continue, we must adopt a policy favouring not only capitalists and large interests, but also encouraging the farmers and labourers.
We are passing through a serious crisis. Now that the Americans have raised their tariff, our farmers can no longer export their products to the United States, the European markets are unimportant and there but remains the local markets. Consequently, the farmers are forced to sell at a sacrifice, their hay, wheat, beef, butter, cheese and all the other products of the farm. Is it not, therefore, reasonable that they should be able to purchase at low prices their farm implements, they who toil so hard and often under very unfavourable conditions, and whose labours have only served, up to now, to enrich manufacturers who benefit from a protection of 35 and even 40 per cent on some farm implements. It is more than time that this state of affairs should cease. Agriculture is, among all industries, the first which should be protected. Our population is made up of 45 per cent of farmers. I well remember that after the Great War when everything was topsy-turvy here as well as in Europe, all our hopes were concentrated on the soil.
"Back to the soil" was our motto. If this be true, the government's policy is quite right in helping the farming class. There is, Sir, another point of view which we must not lose sight of; it is that the lowering of duty will bring down the cost of living. In fact, when the farmer will be in a position to produce cheaper, he will sell his products at a lower price and the labourer will benefit by it.	.	.
I now come to the decrease in taxation. Here, again, our opponents are greatly disappointed. They had dragged the country so much into debt; they had pledged its credit to such an extent, for a number of years to come! No one, I am sure, has forgotten that precious contract which was awarded for the building of ships-for our merchant marine- which have never been of any service and will never be. It was an egregious blunder which cost the country millions of dollars. They had so much encumbered us with the state ownership of railways, that they felt certain that the present government would never find it possible to balance the budget and lower the
taxes. Filled with this hope, the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), with the concurrence of the whole Tory press, started, throughout the country, a campaign of falsehoods, misrepresentations and "whisper of death" spreading everywhere that the King government was incompetent, that Canada was on the brink of bankruptcy, that the national debt was on the increase and that the people could no further bear up with the taxes. And now comes the budget speech which completely reduces to nothing the whole of this dishonourable display and campaign by proclaiming that, thanks to a strict economy, the government has succeeded in lowering the taxes and balancing the budget.
The leader of the opposition was not very prone to remind the people, during the campaign, throughout our provinces, that it was himself and his predecessor, Sir Robert Borden, who, .owing to their imperialist policy and their blind participation in the war, had increased the national debt by two billions and a half of dollars and thereby increased the debt per capita from $47 to $269. The leader of the opposition omitted mentioning, during this campaign, that he was disposed to ruin the country if necessary. His words "to sacrifice the last man and the last dollar to save the Empire" still tingle in our ears. If, while he was imposing blood conscription he had demanded conscription of wealth as Sir Wilfred Laurier suggested; if he had allowed to the manufacturers, who were realizing scandalous profits, but 20 per cent of their profits for administration purposes and if he had obliged them to remit the balance to the treasury, we would now not have to feel the effects of war debts and would thereby have less millionaires in this country; however this would not have suited his political friends.
Now, Sir, ever since the outset of the debate on the budget, the Conservatives have not ceased reproaching the government for having lowered the tariff. Is it an actual fact that this policy of high protection, so much extolled by the right hon. leader of the opposition, is the universal remedy for all our ailments? Is it an actual fact that protection makes for the prosperity of the country and the happiness of the working class? Then, how do we explain, notwithstanding the present tariff, that times are so hard, everybody is complaining, our industries are at a standstill and our people are without work? Is it not rather due to an unfair policy which affords the opportunity to a class of manufacturers of enriching themselves at the expense of the consumers? Is it not a fact that, within a few years, most

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I join those who have preceded me in this debate in extending my regrets that the right honourable the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) was unable to deliver the budget speech of this year. I add the sincere wish that a rapid and complete recovery will soon again enable him to grace this chamber by his presence. On the other hand, if it has been our misfortune to be temporarily deprived of such a capable minister as Mr. Fielding, the generalship of our Prime Minister has given us a second in command who has very ably filled the difficult task imposed upon him. The thanks of this House are due to the hon. the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) for the clear and concise manner in which he has presented to us the annual financial statement of our country and

The Budget-Mr. Black (Huron)
laid before us the changes proposed to our revenue measures.
I do not intend to take up the time of the House with any dissertation on the merits of the respective resolutions to be considered in reference to this year's budget proposals. A better opportunity will be afforded, I believe, to pass judgment upon them when they are being studied in the committee stage, as no doubt the Acting Minister of Finance will' furnish with each resolution, in so far as possible, sufficient statistical information to permit hon. members to appraise the respective measures with due enlightenment. I would suggest to the hon. Acting Minister of Finance that he should be prepared to give this House accurate statistical data or, in cases where this is not available, carefully prepared estimated details as to the number of firms to be affected, their total production, their total capitalization, their total number of employees and their total pay Toll, together with the imports and1 exports by countries of the arteles affected. I believe that this data can easily be prepared. I would even suggest that it would be very advisable to add the expected loss of revenue from measures proposed, giving details as to where the losses and to what amount they will occur. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that if such a statement, was printed and distributed to hon. members before these resolutions are taken up in the committee stage it would enable a much more enlightened discussion and could very reasonably be expected to save considerable of the time of this House.
I desire to limit my remarks to three or four matters which I think deserve serious consideration at the present time. First, however, permit me to take a few minutes to remove from one particular remark of the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) some of the political propaganda which I firmly believe it was intended to spread.
On page 1329 of Hansard of the 14th April, the hon. the ex-Minister of Finance is reported as saying that the reductions proposed to the tariff on agricultural implements would average at best seven dollars. With this statement that this saving of seven dollars per year for each farmer will be the only benefit, I find myself in complete disaccord. In this case the average quoted seems to have been purposely chosen to misrepresent the real benefits that these tariff reductions will have for our farming industry. I do not know the method employed in calculating this average, but I am willing to accept it as representing the correct average. The 
facts of the case, however, cannot be shown by an average saving, because in doing so you are at the same time admitting that the purchase of machinery is evenly distributed. Such is not the case; if it were, the present tariff reductions would be far from possessing the significance that they do undor the real conditions. It is true that seldom a year passes when a farmer can carry on his work without replacing one or another of his implements, but if we only consider the established farm holder how can we expect to solve the economic problems arising from the sparse population at present on our immense territory? How can we expect to entice our young manhood and incoming immigrants to successfully add to our agricultural production by settling new farms? No, Mr. Speaker, the proposed reductions in the tariff are intended to benefit primarily our new settlers and to enable them to equip themselves at as low a cost as possible. I have not calculated what the saving would be on a complete equipment, but I have no hesitation in saying that it certainly will be well in excess of one hundred dollars. Who will say that such a sum wull not be a considerable contribution to the success of our new settlers?
WTe, in this section of the House at least, are very much interested in seeing the large agricultural districts of the northern portions of Ontario and Quebec and the vast unoccupied territory of the western provinces more thickly settled. We realize that by increasing our agricultural production, we shall benefit our manufacturing centres and sanely provide for their expansion. Who will deny that greater population in the rural districts of the West and of the East of this country, greater agricultural production with its necessarily greater demand for manufactured goods, is the real economic necessity that will solve the majority of the problems with which we are struggling to-day. These, and these only, are the considerations that have guided our policy. Hon. members to my right must credit the farming population with very little intelligence when they endeavour to show in this House and outside of it that we are trying to buy our return to this parliament by a paltry consideration to individual farmers, and this at the expense of the manufacturing industry. I repeat that our policy of providing cheaper implements of production is guided by the knowledge that the development of our rural communities will at the same time develop our manufacturing centres and that this combination will spell the success of our Dominion.

The Budget-Mr. Black {Huron).

To what sources can the increased revenue to the Post Office Department be attributed? There are two sources. The first is the increased postal rate in effect since 1915, and the second is the large number of stamp taxes imposed. The Acting Postmaster General has stated that there is no manner of dividing the revenue as between mailing revenue and taxation revenue. One need only recall to mind the many methods other than mailing, with which we have been familiar in the use of stamps, to realize that the revenue derived from these sources must, indeed, be large. I am convinced that a very considerable, if not the greater part of the increased net revenue, which has risen from $13,046,649.57 in 1915 to $29,262,232.78 in 1923, is due to the new stamp taxes. But what do we find as regards total expenditure?-that the total expenditures of the Post Office Department have risen at an alarming rate from $15,961,191.47 in 1915 to $2S,121,533.95 in 1922, and have dropped only some $330,000 to $27,794,501.89 in 1923, Three main factors can increase the expenditures of the Post Office Department. The first is increased work by a large number of mailed packages; the second is increased cost of general salaries, and the third is increased cost of transportation charges. I submit that under none of these headings can you attribute costs against the revenue derived from stamp taxes. The only additional cost to the Post Office Department would be the additional cost of the stamps themselves. Surely the sale of stamps would not add any considerable cost, and we all know that even the cancellation of the stamps so used is outside the field of postal activities. What do those figures tel! us? They tell us a very alarming story and this is it. The net revenue has increased by $16,215,583.21, whereas the total expenditure has increased by $11,833,310.42 between the same two years of 1915 and 1922. leaving a net gain of only $4,382,272.79. Who would attempt to maintain that this amount is all 95

This total of $15,329,624.02 is an average of $1,703,291.56 for this nine year period. The addition of one cent to the postage rate would only need to be paid on 170,329,156 letters each year to produce this average surplus. To realize that the number of mailed letters is far in excess of this amount one need only refer to the number of post offices which was 12,247 in 1922. The total of 170 millions just referred to would average only 13,908 letters per post office per year, or based on a postal year of 310 days only 45 letters per post office per day. Is this not ridiculous? And this calculation, of course, eliminates all mail matter collected on the 3,777 mail routes operated during 1922 with their 202,668 mail boxes. Again, if we only consider the number of three cent stamps issued in 1922-and for what other purpose are three cent stamps used except for the mailing of letters?- we find that the total was 394,869,400. They do, at least, seem to indicate that the standard of efficiency varies according to locality. If we compare Hamilton and Quebec, we find that in the latter city the 171 employees, greater by 59 than in Hamilton, and necessarily requiring larger administrative staffs, the average salary is $1,317.13 or $107.68 smaller than the average of $1,424.81 for Hamilton. Now let us look at the revenue. We find that in Toronto the average revenue per employee is $6,103.17, higher by $1,565.08 than the $4,538.09 for Montreal. This happens with a total number of 950 employees in Toronto as against 811 in Montreal. Between Hamilton and Quebec, the difference is still more marked, the average being $5,252.65 per employee in the Ontario city as against $3,058.63 in the latter place. The difference in favour of Hamilton is $2,194.02; and in this instance we find that the highest average revenue is for Hamilton where the number of employees is 59 less than for the city of Quebec. Now, Mr. Speaker, is it reasonable to believe that the figures and averages I have just quoted in reference to four important post offices are such as to convince us that the management of our postal service has attained that high plane of efficiency which is claimed for it? On the contrary, if reclassi-

fication .and reorganization have produced results such as these figures indicate. I am of the opinion that the work has fallen far short of meriting praise of any kind and that they should furnish sufficient incentive for a determined effort to rectify the anomalous conditions shown to exist.
All the figures I have quoted have been taken from answers given to this House by the Acting Postmaster General or
4 p.m. from the annual reports of the Auditor General. And I may remark, Mr. Speaker, that the figures shown for net revenue and total expenditures in the Auditor General's reports differ greatly, as to the expenditures, from those furnished by the Acting Postmaster General. I need only quote the expenditures for 1922, which the Auditor General shows as $32,003,188.92, as against $28,121,533.06 given by the Acting Postmaster General, and $31,180,184.40 as against $27,794,501.89 for 1923. I do not know why there should be such a difference. Let us hope that the Auditor General is wrong in this case. Otherwise the total surplus of $15,329,624.02 for the nine year period as shown from the figures of the Acting Postmaster General would be turned to a total deficit of $9,890,954.07. I trust however that the Acting Postmaster General will take note of these figures and furnish us with an explanation as to the reason for the variation. When we consider, Mr. Speaker, that there

The Budget-Mr. Black {Huron).
were in 1922 in Canada 4,451 branches of banks and that at an average of only 50 cheques per branch per day for a banking year of 300 days they would handle 66,765,000 cheques, on each one of which there would need to be at least one two-cent stamp, and that stamps are also required for receipts, for notes and for many other purposes of taxation, we cannot help but conclude that the average surplus of $1,703,291.56 is very far below the actual taxation imposed in stamp taxes on the Canadian public. Notwithstanding the increase of one cent in the ordinary postal rate and the doubling of the registration fee, our postal system has been operated at a great loss during the last nine years. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the apparent surplus of $1,467,730.89 shown for 1923 by the figures of the Acting Postmaster General would be turned into a deficit of many millions of dollars were it possible to eliminate all but actual postal revenue. Surely there is urgent need for an immediate rectification of these conditions. Under present day taxation, when a tax of some kind meets us at every corner; when the interest charges on our huge national debt account in themselves for a greater total than all our expenditures at the beginning of this century, we can ill afford to operate at a loss a service which produced surpluses in the days of low taxation.
We have in recent years, Mr. Speaker, heard both criticisms and praise of the civil service of this country-criticism mostly of the conditions existing in the service and, in rare cases, against civil servants themselves. The praise, on the other hand, was for the far greater part given the civil servants and was in a sense a tribute to their individual efficiency, to rare achievements or to undoubted ability in transacting the public business. This session the government came to us with loud heralding of the reductions they were going to carry on in the civil service, in order to eliminate duplication of work, do away with overmanning, increase efficiency and decrease expenditures. The estimates we have been studying do not indicate any very great progress in that direction this year, and I may say I am rather glad of it. Mr. Speaker, I fully realize that we are traversing a period of financial stress in this country and that there was never a greater need for economy. But I also believe that we cannot hope to achieve efficiency and low costs in our civil service by the process of haphazard elimination which has been practised this year. I mean the reduction of staff here and there with the consequent chopping off of this or that particular 95i
piece of work. Furthermore, I do not believe there is a single hon. member in this House, and probably it would be difficult to find a single elector in the country, who, if he knew all the conditions, would want us to economize to the extent of a few dollars in the civil service at the expense of our contracts, written, verbal or implied, with the employees of this Dominion. It is not fair, nay, it is criminal, to engage young men or young girls, keep them for many years, oblige them to train in a line of work which only the government does, and then release them with little or no compensation when it had been more or less definitely understood that the employment would continue as long as the services rendered were efficient and the employee continued his good behaviour, Take the young man who enters the service at a low salary, gives of his best at small remuneration, and by constant application to his work attains a somewhat higher salary rate. He has chosen the service as a career and fitted himself for a particular line of work different from what is required by other employers. I claim that it is not fair to dismiss him after he has passed up chances of being successful in other work in order to accept government employment, often at a much lower salary on the consideration that the work would be permanent.
No, Mr. Speaker, efficiency, removal of overmanning and consequent economy will never be obtained by the method which has been employed in the service this year. Unless a proper system is adopted and worked consistently we can never hope to have better conditions than we have to-day. Can any one honestly claim that civil servants are responsible for the conditions that exist? Is it the fault of the employee when the employer engages him to perform work already being done in another department or for which there is no need? Is it the fault of the employee if the hours of labour are limited to six and one half on week days and four on Saturdays? No, the responsibility for the conditions found to-day lies at the feet of the governments, both present and past. It is the duty of the government to rectify these conditions, and I say that it is also their bounden duty to do so without causing any hardship to the civil servants who have only been the dupes of maladministration, extravagance and political patronage. I dare say that the reductions which are taking place this year will still leave a condition, in permanent departments at least, worse than existed when the government of to-day took office. I mean that I believe the number of appointments in excess of retirements from all causes has been much greater
1488	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Black {Huron).
since 1922 than the reductions which are taking place this year. There is one method and only one, by which better conditions can be made to prevail in the civil service of this country, and I would suggest this method for the serious consideration of the government:
1.	A complete survey of the work to be performed with a view to eliminating all duplication of work and expense.
2.	The gradual installation of all modem labour-saving facilities so that the greatest amount of work can be performed with the least possible staff.
3.	The complete cessation of appointments until overmanning has completely disappeared; With the exception only of technical requirements when investigation has shown that no one within the civil service possesses the necessary qualifications.
4.	The filling of all vacancies through transfers from one department to another.
5.	An arrangement by which the civil servants would contribute sufficient of their annual salaries to permit of a reasonable superannuation system without adding to the cost of civil government.
6.	The gradual increase, according to reduction in total staff, of the hours of labour from six and one half as at present to at least seven and one half or eight hours.
7.	A. thorough, study of salary conditions in order that proper remuneration schedules can be adopted so as to furnish proper incentive for efficient service.
8.	No dismissals, exeept for bad behaviour or inefficient services; as well as in those cases where the appointment has been of a purely temporary nature.
9.	The establishment of a consulting group chosen from civil servants themselves to help the government to bring about the necessary changes.
In connection with the last suggestion, there is not a shade of doubt in my mind that if ministers, deputy ministers and the Civil Service Commission thoroughly co-operated with a well chosen body of civil servants, results of a permanent nature would be more quickly achieved than through the adoption of any other method.
I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that the above plan, if followed, will bring about permanent results, will cause hardship to no one, and should remove for all time from the mind of every one the far too frequent cry of mismanagement which is being heard these days. I repeat that civil servants have not in any way been responsible for the conditions that exist to-day, that the governments, both present and past, must shoulder the responsibil-

ity and that any policy whereby the innocent must suffer is unfair and unjust and betrays that spirit of British justice of which we are all so proud. I trust that the government will take kindly to my suggestions, and give them serious consideration.
I now come, Mr. Speaker, to the last part of my remarks. We have been accused of representing only one element of this country. It is often stated that we are only interested in the measures that will be of immediate benefit to the farming community of Canada; that we are willing to sacrifice the interests of other sections provided that the farmers' desires are served. Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that if such were our policies we would not deserve the name of Canadians. No, such are not our policies. We are, on the contrary, interested in the welfare and progress of Canada as a whole, in the progress of our manufacturing industries as well as in the welfare of our farming communities. We desire conditions in this country which will permit suitable living and working conditions to obtain for our farm labourers and farmers, as well as for the artisans of our urban centres and our manufacturers. The movement responsible for our presence in this chamber, however, was based on the unfair conditions that have long existed against the farmers of this Dominion, due, no doubt, to their practical lack of representation in the parliament of our country previous to the last election. Such an important section was entitled to a hearing in this Palace of Laws and surely no one would maintain that in devising our legislation their welfare should not be taken into account. To-day unfair conditions exist,, and our efforts are directed to equalize conditions as between all sections, in so far as possible.
How can farmers be satisfied with conditions such as are disclosed in the March, 1924, issue of the Prices and Price Index Bulletin of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, where it is shown, for example, that the index number for grains has risen from 100 in 1913 to 124.9 in 1923, and that the index number for flour and milled products made from these same grains has risen from 100 to 131.1 between the same two years, but that, on the other hand, the tea, coffee, cocoa and spices that the farmers must buy had risen to 201.0 in 1923 as against 100 in 1913; that the vegetables he sold at 100 in 1913 brought him 157.7 in 1923, but that the hosiery for which he disbursed 100 in 1913 cost him 295.2 in 1923? ' Can he be expected to remain inactive in the face of the index price for hides, for instance, which dropped from 100 in 1913 to 80.9 in 1923, whilst the leather made from

The Budget-Mr. Black (Huron).
these hides has risen from 100 to 116.3 between the same two years, a difference against the farmer of 35.4? And going a step further, he finds that boots and shoes, again the product of the hides, have risen to 141.9 in 1923 from the base of 100 in 1913. Has not the farmer just cause for complaint when a ten-year period places him at a disadvantage of 60 points between the hides that he produces and the shoes he must buy? The same i conditions, Mr. Speaker, apply in the same manner to all the farmer has to sell as compared to what he has to buy. In every instance, practically, the increases which have taken place in the prices of the commodities which he requires are very much greater than the increased prices which he receives for his produce. And in some cases there have been actual decreases in the prices which he receives. The bulletin to which I refer uses a base of 100 for the year 1913 and we find figures such as these for 1923: tools and hand implements, 212.6, bricks, 169.0, lime and cement, 159.6, sugar and its products, 226.4, woollen cloth, hosiery and underwear, 233.3 and so on all along the line of the goods the farmer must buy. But if we look at the 1923 index numbers of the goods he has to sell the story is very much different and it is at once apparent that his revenues have far from kept pace with his increased costs of living and of production. Live stock dropped to 97.6, hides and skins to 80.9, whilst grains have only risen to 124.9, eggs to 130.1-those are last year's figures; eggs have dropped this year* 50 per cent- and vegetables, from which in the great majority of cases no revenue is derived by the ordinary farmer, to 157.7.
If we analyse price conditions from another angle we find that the wholesale prices show that wheat was at 88 cents per bushel in 1913 and 81.08 a bushel in 1923, but we also find that a barrel of flour could be purchased for S5.36 in 1913 and that it cost $6.87 in 1923. Now, Mr. Speaker, based on the average of four and one half bushels of wheat to a barrel of flour, we find that between 1913 and 1923 the farmer received 90 cents more for the wheat necessary to produce a barrel of flour, but that when he had to purchase that flour the cost to him increased by SI.51 or an adverse balance of 61 cents against the farmer. Everywhere you look you find the same results. Cattle brought $6.89 a hundredweight in 1913 and only $6.80 in 1923. But sugar cost $9.58 against $4.18 in 1913. There is no need of quoting more, suffice it to say that no matter from what direction you look at these official figures you always arrive at the same conclusion, that is, the
farmer pays more for all he needs, and in many cases receives less for what he has to sell, and in no case is the increase to him proportionate to the increase against him.
Can we reasonably expect contentment when such conditions prevail? Can we be blamed for our endeavours to bring about more normal conditions? Surely not, more equitable conditions are urgently required, and until they obtain there can be no real progress. Hon. members to my right have been painting blue ruin for the manufacturers of this country unless we keep our hands off the tariff. Yes, indeed, they endeavour to maintain that rather than a lowering of the tariff we are in urgent need of higher tariff barriers, if we do not wish our manufacturing industry to go into bankruptcy. Mr. Speaker, higher tariffs, and in fact tariffs of any kind, can only bring artificial life to any industry and they never will solve the problems of the manufacturers. Their troubles lie elsewhere. They must pare down their overhead charges, they must lessen their sales costs, they must cheapen the extremely expensive distribution system existing to-day, and they must realize that business expansion can only take place on sound foundations and not on artificial tariff proppings, if they expect to bring a permanent cure to the ills of which they are complaining.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I wish to repeat that the dissatisfaction and unrest amongst our farming classes is due to the unfair conditions which I have endeavoured to portray. Farmers have a vital interest in the expansion of our manufacturing industries, and their Canadianism is of a brand that extends far beyond the bounds of class selfishness. They realize that true progress cannot be local in its scope. And our efforts to bring about more equitable conditions, are based on the absolute conviction that an adjustment of the unfair conditions of to-day will prove to be the required impetus for true progress for all classes and in every corner of our wonderful Dominion.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to rise to a point of order. I desire to submit to you, in all respect, that the amendment of the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) is not in order and cannot be considered. The amendment as read by the Chair is as follows:
That all the words after "that1' be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
Whereas the budget proposals would seem to indicate the recognition by the government of the necessity for a fiscal policy designed to encourage industries based upon the development of the natural resources of the country, and to afford some alleviation of the financial burdens bearing upon the people;

Point oj. Order-Mr. Meighen
a minister. Bjr way of illustration I read one of the resolutions which now stands in the name of the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham), a resolution as to the construction of a railway. He does not move a resolution which, if it passes, of itself means that a road is to be built, which of itself makes any charge on the people or any loss to the treasury. Not at all. He simply moves a resolution which says "it is expedient." What is the difference between the word "desirable" and the word "expedient?" Is one more general than the other? Is one more specific than the other? Is one abstract and the other not? In that regard both are identical. The minister moves a resolution which reads:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide for the construction of a Canadian National Railway line, jointly with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, from Rosedale...
And so on. That it is "expedient" to do so. Now we say that it is "desirable" to tax all unearned incomes more. Is that merely an abstract, pious affirmation? It means this, that if this House approves, the House directs that a bill be introduced to that effect. If this step can be taken on thq motion of an hon. member who is not a member of the government, then I submit very seriously that we are simply playing fast and loose with the rules of this House; that there is no place to stop; that the rule which has come down through generations in the British House and which has proven a safeguard of their parliament, is to be abandoned by us. Because, if we can move that it is desirable to do a certain thing, even for the moment appropriating the language of the amended resolution, on the motion of a private member, and put the House on its judgment, then all this safeguard is gone. We can move that it is expedient to do a certain thing or we can use any other adjective we like. So I submit most earnestly, out of the regard which I have for the rules of this House and for the future conduct of this parliament, that this motion of the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) is clearly and unqualifiedly out of order.
Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Centre Win-mpeg). Mr. Speaker, I think it is, perhaps, a little strange that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) gave me no notice whatever that he proposed to take action at this time.

I would urge that this is a question of giving notice of a matter that is already before the House. I am under absolutely no obligation to give notice of any motion of mine to the leader of one of the other parties of this House. So again I would say that it would seem as if there might have been some notice given that this matter was to come before the House at this time. I might also call attention to the fact that the leader of the opposition in the earlier part of his remarks proceeded to read me a lecture as to my reasons and motives for preparing such a motion as this, and he also rather implied that there had been changes that had been, perhaps, almost underhand in their character. I should like to make a very brief statement as to the character of the alterations that were made. In the very first place, I should like to ask that the scroll of the House should be produced on this occasion as I believe it was a few days ago, in order that we may see just where we stand in the matter. My resolution, as the leader of the opposition has stated, is given in Hansard at page 1460. Immediately after recess, before the motion had been accepted or read to the House, it was suggested to me by the Speaker that possibly the form was not the best and that it might be modified in order that it might more nearly conform with the regularly accepted rules of the House. In consultation with the Speaker and the authorities of this House, I consented to make such changes in the resolution as seemed to be necessary	or advisable in order that
it should conform more nearly with the accepted usages of the House. That is precisely how the matter stands with regard to that point. I thought I was on safe ground in introducing the resolution, since in form I followed a resolution which was introduced a year ago by the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) on May 14, 1923, as reported on page 2717 of Hansard. Mr. Forke moved:
That all the words after the word " that " be struck out, and the following be substituted therefor: Whereas the tariff policy of the government, as indicated by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech, and particularly his pronouncement in favour of tariff stability at existing rates, and the consequent intimation that the government contemplates no further appreciable tariff reduction, constitutes a repudiation of the tariff planks in the Liberal platform of 1919 and is inconsistent with the Finance Minister's statement last session that the changes then made were a step in the right direction;
And, whereas, the fiscal policy of the government as now brought down is based on the principles of protection, and in this respect is indistinguishable from that of their predecessors in office;

Point oj Order-Mr. Marcil (Bonaventure)
And whereas the condition of the primary industries and the position of consumers in general is such as to demand immediate relief;
Therefore, be it resolved:	That while recognizing
that changes in the fiscal policy should be made in such a way as to give industries affected a reasonable opportunity for readjustment, this House is of the opinion that the principle of protection as a basis for fiscal policy in Canada is unsound, and that every claim for protection should be heard publicly before a special committee of parliament.
And, further, that the best interests of Canada will be served by:-
(a)	An immediate and substantial reduction in the tariff, particularly on the necessaries of life and the implements of production.
(b)	An immediate increase in the British preference to 50 per cent of the general tariff.
(c)	Reciprocity in trade with the United States as outlined in the proposed Reciprocity Agreement of 1911.
And, further, that the loss of revenues, if any, which might result from a reduction in customs duties should be made good by:-
(a)	The readjustment and extension * of the income tax to bear more heavily on unearned incomes.
(b)	The increase and extension of excise and other taxes on luxuries.
If you will compare the resolution as I presented it to the House with that which was presented a year ago by the leader of the Progressives, you will find that the form is exactly similar. Some of the clauses are taken word for word. The leader of the opposition quotes a number of authorities and various precedents to show that it is impossible that a resolution in this form should be accepted by the House. The fact is that a resolution in this form was accepted a year ago, and I ask:	If this could
be accepted a year ago by the House when moved by the leader of the Progressives, why cannot my resolution be accepted this year? Surely, this is a precedent. I am not going into any detail as to the form of the resolution or whether it conforms exactly with the principle suggested by the authorities on procedure. It seems to me that it would be a very serious thing, indeed, for the conduct of the business of this House if private members are not to be permitted to introduce resolutions dealing with the underlying principles of taxation. It would simply reduce to impotence the entire opposition and we should not be able to submit any constructive suggestions whatever. I take it that if this resolution were passed the effect would be virtually the adoption of a certain principle, and it would then be open to the government to bring down such special measures along that line as they might see fit. As I have not had any opportunity of consulting the authorities on this matter I think, Mr. Speaker, that with your consent and with the permission of the House it might be desirable that this debate should be adjourned until I have had such opportunity.

Mr. ALEXANDRE J. DOUCET (Kent, N.B.): May I at the outset join with the many hon. members who deplore the fact that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) could not be present to deliver the budget this year. As a member from the Maritime provinces, born in Nova Scotia, I regret that by reason of ill-health he has been unable so far to attend the present session of par-

liament. Had he been privileged to deliver the budget I am sure that he would have weighed the consequences seriously before bringing down a budget that has caused consternation throughout the country. He would have borne in mind what occurred in parliament on April 22, 1897, and would no doubt have seen to it that his budget would be so framed as to satisfy as far as possible all sections and classes of the Dominion. All hon. gentlemen who have so far spoken from the government benches have maintained that agriculture stands to benefit largely from the reduction in what is called the protective tariff. I, Sir, representing a constituency whose interests are centered in agriculture, in the fisheries, and in lumber, fail to see how a reduction in the tariff as submitted by the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) is going to be of such great advantage to the people. The hon. member for Kings, N.S., (Mr. Robinson), speaking yesterday on this question, justified his purpose to support the budget by the fact that, as he said, his constituents would be relieved of present burdens inasmuch as fertilizers were going to be 5 p.m. exempt from duty. My hon.
friend must know, surely, that his constituents who are engaged in the raising of fruit, and the fruit companies in the whole valley of the Annapolis, have been accustomed to bring in fertilizers in the unmixed state to be mixed and compounded at home.
The ingredients necessary in the manufacture of fertilizer, such as nitrate of soda, muriate of potash and sulphate of ammonia, have been coming into this country duty free. It is true that ground acid phosphate was subject to a tax of 20 per cent, while phosphate rock, unground phosphate, could be imported free. But if the farmers or the fruit growers of any section of the Dominion had to import phosphoric acid in its ground state, that would mean a duty of 20 per cent on each ton value of $12, and as the amount of acid phosphate required for the fertilizing of one acre of orchard is 300 pounds, the hon. member for Kings N.S. (Mr. Robinson) feels justified in supporting the present budget because it does save his constituents 36 cents an acre in fertilizer. I do not believe that the reduction of tariff is going to be a panacea for all the ills, the dissatisfaction and the unrest that prevail to-day among the agricultural classes. And when I speak, Sir, of agricultural classes, I do not refer to the wheat miners, to those who for years have been mining the soil of this Dominion; I speak of the class referred to by the Minister of Agriculture as those en-

The Budget-Mr. Doucet
gaged in diversified farming. We in the Maritime provinces call it mixed farming, and we get so much mixed up in trying to make both ends meet that I think we shall continue to call it mixed farming.
Now, some of our friends from the eastern section of the country, and possibly from the Pacific section as well, Will claim that they are justified in voting for the budget because it means a large reduction in the cost of those things which are necessary in the fishing industry. Why, they say, everything needed in the pursuit of that industry will be duty free, but they take good care not to tell their constituents and the public in general that with the exception of tarred marlin everything used in that industry was already free.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Conditions to-day are such throughout the length and breadth of this Dominion that it is not the time to be meddling with tariffs or to institute any policy which would be detrimental to any one section or to any one industry. In this connection I want to cite a few figures to show that the farming industry, one of the basic industries of this Dominion, is in such a position that it needs more than a little whittling of the protective tariff. The live stock statistics for 1921 and 1923 are, to my mind, conclusive evidence of the fact that all is not well with the agricultural industry. In 1923 there was a decrease of 283,280 horses in the country as compared with the figure for 1921. There was also a decrease of 799,636 in the number of cattle. There was a decrease also of 921,993 in the number of sheep, and an increase of 550,421 in the number of swine. That increase must have been due to the effort of the farmer to bring about, the consumption of their over-production of agricultural produce, an over-production due to the supplanting of their products by those which are coming into this country from across the line. But although there was an increase of over 550,000 in the number of swine, the value of that particular line of live stock decreased by $1,730,000. The total number of heads of live stock was 1,615,730 less in 1923 than it was in 1921, and the total value decreased by $152,704,000. That is sufficient evidence to show that something
is wrong. For this condition the high cost of transportation is largely responsible; we have not the proper market facilities, and there is an importation of American produce which operates to our detriment. At present eggs are coming across the line in direct competition with our own produce. I am told that in the city of St. John storage eggs were offered last week for 7 cents a dozen. Now, I want to be fair; I do not believe storage eggs were offered at St. John at that price, but I believe that quotations were made to St. John wholesale merchants for American storage eggs at 7 cents a dozen. That is not improbable, because the duty on eggs imported into this country is only 3 cents a dozen while the duty on eggs exported from Canada to the United States is 8 cents a dozen.
Agricultural conditions are not as we would like to see them in the province from which I come, as is shown by the statistics furnished by the provincial Department of Agriculture. During the year 1923 the acreage of our four important crops, wheat, oats, turnips and potatoes, was 131,107 acres less than in the year 1922, and we account for that decrease in acreage by the fact that there were 10,735 more farms vacanc in 1923 than in 1922; in other words, only 77 per cent of the cultivated farms of 1922 were cultivated in 1923. and that, Sir. without going into details, explains the large exodus of our population from the province of New Brunswick. I venture to say, Sir, that if I had the statistics before me I would find that the same rule applies to half the provinces of the Dominion, at least from the centre to the Atlantic ocean
But, of course, Mr. Speaker, this great budget and the tariff proposals that have been brought down are going to be a panacea that will cure all evils, and with that policy in force we must expect conditions to become rosy. Sir, I submit that the most important factor in connection with the future of our agricultural interests in this Dominion is to find a home market for our produce. I am not so much concerned about the implement manufacturers in the centre of this Dominion, but I submit that if we wish to create and develop a home market for the purpose of providing consumers for the products of our farms we must have a certain measure of protection, for the industrial centres, and I submit that when you are whittling off the duty on farm implements, and are allowing bar steel, bar iron, and pig , iron and other semi-finished products to come into this country for the purpose of
The Budget-Mr. Doucet

manufacturing farm implements, you are striking a death blow to one of our largest industries in eastern Canada. We have in that section of the country an industry that was fostered by both governments. It was the result of the national policy and continued by those who followed the Liberal-Conservative administration of 1896. It was the result of a system of bonusing the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, the purpose of which was to place them in a position to compete in the markets of this Dominion with their bigger competitors in the United States. That bonus was withdrawn, it is true, but to-day besides withdrawing the bonus, when this government withdraws the protection they have enjoyed when they came into direct competition with the products of the United States, favoured by a shorter haul, it strikes a blow, and a stunning blow at that industry which provides a large market for a great portion of the agricultural products of the Maritime provinces.
I did expect, Sir, after the eloquent, sincere, earnest and honest appeal made by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) that we would have seen some encouragement given in this budget to the coal industry. Not he alone is interested in placing a protective tariff on bituminous coal entering this county, the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. Kelly), who moved the Address in reply to the Speech . from the Throne, and the hon. members for Cape Breton South and Richmond (Messrs. Carroll and Ivyte), together with the hon. member who occupies the position of Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald), are all greatly interested in the coal industry.
I do not cite anyone to my left as representing the coal mining industries of Alberta, because I do not know the exact portion of the province in which coal may be mined out there, but I do say that in the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick we have vast limits of coal mines, and that industry could be developed to the point of supplying our share or fifty per cent of the bituminous coal imported from the United States. Of the 16,000,000 tons of coal imported, we could supply our portion, 8,000,000 tons, and that on the basis of $8 per ton would mean that for the mining of the coal and the labour connected therewith, for its transportation from the pit mouth to the manufacturing centres of the Dominion and to the consumers of Ontario and Quebec, we would have the tidy sum of $64,000,000 spread all over the country from Cape Breton right up [DOT] to Toronto and Brockville. I submit, Sir,

this is a matter of vast importance, and having been first suggested by a member supporting the government, the hon. member for Cumberland, a protective tariff should have been placed on coal. We have to-day a tariff of 13 cents per ton on slack coal. That duty was put on when slack coal could be bought at the pit mouth for 75 cents a ton; to-day slack coal sells at the pit mouth for $2.85. Is that a fair comparison? Again, we have a protective tariff of 53 cents a ton on run-of-mine coal. That specific duty of 53 cents a ton was put on when run-of-mine coal was selling for $1.25 per ton; to-day it sells for something like $3.75.
But apart from any protection that might have been afforded by the tariff, I think we might have had a suggestion from the government side of the House for a special transportation rate for the purpose of transporting our fuel. That would only have been in harmony with the resolution passed by this House in favour of a national system of fuel supply.
The hon. member for Hull (Mr. Fontaine), who spoke this afternoon-before referring to his speech I might suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the members of this House, that in addition to the suggestion I made here some time ago, the name of the hon. member for Hull might be added to that famous committee to inquire how best to bring about national unity in this Dominion. My hon. friend's utterances this afternoon in connection with the visit of my honoured leader to the province of Quebec will make very good reading. I would suggest to those who framed the Liberal platform of 1919, and who profess to be so anxious to bring about national unity to this country, that the reading of this speech, when it has been translated will be very edifying indeed, and a source of great benefit to the whole Dominion. I need not dwell any longer upon the question. The House and the country know my stand with respect to it. I have nothing whatever to withdraw and I shall never lose an opportunity of pointing out, here or elsewhere, that such arguments as those of my hon. friend are not conducive to the best interests of Canada.
My hon. friend professed himself greatly pleased because the budget was going to relieve the agricultural class. Now, I have shown how those classes are not going to be relieved to any extent in the matter of fertilizers. The question may be asked:	Will
they not be relieved with respect to farming implements? I maintain that the greatest bugbear of the farming population to-day- especially where we have mixed farming, I

The Budget-Mr. Doucet
stick to that expression, Sir, for a reason- is that we have too many farming implements. The state of the market is such that production does not pay, and it is a question of keeping those implements utilized all the time.
I may say this, however, regarding certain sections of the country that I know of:	If
they would only place their agricultural implements under cover in the fall of the year, taking them out when needed in the spring, they would certainly save more than any whittling of the protective tariff is going to accomplish. [DOT]
My hon. friend told the House that the labouring classes in his constituency would benefit greatly by the reduction in the tariff. It would be interesting to know how they will benefit. Even if there was a slight possibility of a reduction in the cost of living would not the labouring classes of the Dominion prefer to have a full week's pay rather than be idle half the time as will be the case by tariff changes, or mooted tariff changes, throwing the industrial centres into consternation.
I have spoken on the question of transportation, and I should like to say a word or two further with respect to it inasmuch as it vitally affects the section of Canada from which I come. In discussing the question I shall endeavour to treat it from a national standpoint. We have been termed "whiners" in the Maritime provinces so often by the press, and I think the epithet has also been used by hon. members here, that I should like to point out that the question is one of national interest. Transportation, owing to geographical reasons, is of the utmost importance to the Maritime provinces. Certain traffic rates must be granted and adhered to if our natural resources are to have any chance at all of reaching the markets of the central provinces. No special privileges are desired by the fishing industry of the Maritime provinces but it does wish to have a fair opportunity of marketing its products in Quebec and Ontario, and other provinces. Such is not the case to-day. In the eyes of the public the Atlantic region is being discriminated against by the National Railways and is not getting its fair share of what it should enjoy. On the 10th instant, as will be found by reference to page 1207 of Hansard, the Minister of Railways stated in reply to questions that the operating expenses of the Atlantic region for the year 1923 exceeded the operating revenue in the same region by $5,222,145; for the western region there was a deficit of $2,020,/09; and' that in the central region there was
a huge surplus of $18,687,610. Hon. gentlemen, and the public in general, may understand that possibly there is a reason for the deficit in the western section in view of the prevailing rates for the carriage of grain. I have no fault to find because special concessions are given for the transportation of grain, if, even at a loss to the railways. It is one of our basic industries and is entitled to certain concessions and rightly so. But the question is asked, why there should be a deficit in the Atlantic region. The answer to that question is very simple. The deficit exists because the railway system is overmanned, bearing in mind the extent of its mileage. To-day you will find at headquarters at Moncton practically the same staff that existed prior to 1921-22 when the Atlantic region consisted of the Intercolonial and all branch lines into Montreal, and the Transcontinental. Not only is a large staff still maintained but in some cases the salaries of the staff, as a result of recommendations made by the new board have doubled and trebled. Now, a question was placed on the order paper on two different occasions with a view to eliciting .certain information. That information was withheld on the ground that to give it was not in the public interest, although it was very necessary if any real comparison was sought to be made of the administrative expenses in 1921-22 compared with the expenses to-day.	I ask why
that information was withheld, especially when it is borne in mind that the Auditor General's report next year will contain all the information that was asked for by the two	returns in question?
But it will then be too late. That information is withheld for some purpose or for some reason. Let me tell the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) and this House that this information is demanded and will be sought for, and when the proper time comes those who are responsible for withholding that information will feel the effect of ignoring public opinion. The electors of this Dominion are shareholders of the Canadian National Railways. The members of parliament are the elected board of directors. The government in council or the cabinet is the executive appointed by the board of directors. The fact that they have transferred the administration of their authority to another independent body does not to my mind relieve them from direct responsibility to the country and to the shareholders for the administration of the road. We as the shareholders of this railway have the right to know how much the administration of each and every section of the road has cost the country. May I, Mr. Speaker, tell you
The Budget-Mr. Doucet

why the information is withheld? It is because there has been discrimination in the appointment of officials in the Atlantic region. That discrimination has taken place, and it is very important that the fact should be made known, so that the proper charges against those responsible might be made on the floor of this House, if need be. Some day soon all the information refused will be obtained. The majority of the government supporters who have spoken on the budget have complimented Sir Henry Thornton on the great ability he has displayed in the administration of the Canadian National Railways. I do not wish to detract from the ability of that gentleman, but I am reminded a good deal of a merchant in a small town who, every time he was asked to contribute to any church or any charitable object, would immediately place a half a cent a pound on the price of his sugar or some other very necessary commodity, and before twenty-four hours had elasped he had more than doubled the contribution he had made to the charitable institution. Every time the president of the Canadian National Railways tells us-and he does it openly and publicly-that there has been a saving, and that we are going to have a surplus, it would be advisable to investigate, and we many find before twenty-four hours have elasped that Sir Henry Thornton and his executive staff have curtailed some public service on that road, in order to make certain economies.

speechtext: Does the hon. member mean to say that the public service on the Canadian National road has been depleted?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes. The county I represent is not very far from the home of the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud). He may have occasion to travel over my constituency, and I wish to remind him that while, for the last 34 years there has been a daily train service on the Moncton and Buc-touche railway for 32 miles, and for the last 28 years a daily mail service on that road, since the 6th January, 1924, no train is run on Wednesdays, and the residents along that road for 32 miles have not the benefit of their daily mail on Wednesday. I say that is depleting or curtailing public service in so far as the Moncton and Buctouche railway is concerned. There are only 32 miles of government railway in the constituency which I have the honour to represent. I feel that it is my bounden duty to myself and to my constituents to set the hon. member for Gloucester right, and to tell the public at large that we intend to protest that there should be no curtailment of the public service of the 
Canadian National Railways in order to give Sir Henry Thornton or any other man the privilege of declaring economy in the service. True we have the satisfaction of knowing that the radio has been installed, and I say in all earnestness and sincerity that it must be a great comfort to the farmers and fishermen of Kent county. But these people are being deprived of the daily trips on Wednesday and cannot read the daily paper on Wednesday evening, in order that Sir Henry Thornton and other titled men may talk all night over the benefit of radio to the province, when we in Kent county can not get public service. It may be noticeable that the radio system is for the benefit of two regions only, and that we have no installation of any kind in the Atlantic section. As usual the Atlantic section gets 'he short end of it. Sir Henry Thornton is not alone to be blamed for the administration of this railway. It is true he is president of the board, and not only does he administer the railway in his own way, but he acts also as political interpreter of the Dominion. Hon. members might have noticed in the press that after the reverses on the 6th and 20th December last, Sir Henry Thornton gave his own version as to why the Maritime provinces were dissatisfied. Sir Henry Thornton, when assuming the responsibility of president of the Canadian National Railway board, should not have discriminated against the Atlantic section of that road. We had reason to believe, and we have yet reason to believe, that the Atlantic section has a right to have service on the Intercolonial and all branch lines from Sydney, Halifax and Yarmouth to Montreal, and to connect with the Grand Trunk into Portland. Nothing short of that would satisfy the Maritime provinces. We have one-tenth of the mileage to-day, some 2,283 miles. In that section we have two large grain elevators, one of which has not been used at all for the last two years, and we have the Prince Edward Island ferry which is, I believe, a source of deficit, but we make no complaint as to that. If we gave that province a public service we should be proud of it and satisfied with it. But I say that with two great terminal elevators and the Prince Edward Island ferry, and a number of wharves on the Halifax and South Western Railway, built by Mackenzie and Mann, we have enormous expenditures and we have not the railway system to give us the revenue. Hence it is when the answer is given to us that there is a deficit of over $5,000,000, it is not because we do not have the freight for the roads, but because we do not have the mileage.
I	do not intend to delay this House any longer.

I might read to the House the note I have concerning this:
In 1919 when a conflict of railway routes between the Canadian National Railways and Canadian Pacific Railway was discussed before the Board of Railway Commissioners, for a line easterly out of the Drum-heller coal fields down the Red Deer river, the board ruled that this should become a joint line with equal rights to each railway, and that the parties should make an agreement covering the same. This resulted in an agreement, May 9th, 1919, being drawn, making the stretch east from Rosedale as far as Bullpound Creek an equal joint section and fixing certain limitations in reference to the balance of the route.
The Canadian Pacific Railway now wish to proceed with this joint section construction.
This line will open a further area of the Drumheller coal fields. From the end of the joint section this line when finally linked up easterly to the Acadia valley line will afford the Canadian National Railways lighter grades eastbound for coal from the Drumheller fields. It will also serve the agricultural district on either side of the Red Deer river over this distance.
No final running rights agreement has been reached with the Canadian Pacific Railway as to the detailed terms for the use of the joint section, but the estimate is based on the understanding that half the money will be provided by each party.
Mr. MEIGHEN':	Is there any one who

I wish to
take a little time to-night to discuss in a general way this branch line programme. There have been a number of statements made from across the floor of the House and also from my right with regard to the value of the western lines in general to the Canadian National Railways, and it has been suggested by some hon. members that this branch line programme was a means of purchasing Progressive support for the government, and that there is really no justification from a financial standpoint for this construction. I do not want to quote the various statements I have here that were made in the House- the statement, for instance, by the hon. member for Joliette, another by the hon. member for South Oxford, and another by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, with regard to the question of duplication. The ex-Minister of Finance the other day after the budget was introduced read from a return that had been. brought down with regard to the railways especially the National Railways, and this is what he said:
There \yas a time when our railways in western territory were good assets, but we have got a return to-day by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. APRIL 25, 1924

The hon. acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) talks about the great increase of industrial and agricultural activity that his measure will produce. Why, we have never had a bigger or better year, so far as volume is concerned, than the present year; and yet the whole earnings of all the western territories, the prairie provinces and British Columbia, for the last year amount to $72,000,000 and the operating expenses amount to $74,000,000.

But if we compare the newer railways in the West with the newer railways in the eastern and central regions, we find that against a net operating loss in the West of $2,000,000 there is a net operating loss in the East-that is, taking the central region and the Atlantic region together-of $4,000,000. So it would seem, from this return, that the western lines are justified in spite of the statements that have been made in this debate to the effect that the East was paying for the western lines.
I would like to point out that included in the western division is a large section of Ontario. The western region comes east as far as Armstrong, Ontario, and we have two main lines running about 300 miles east, making a total of 625 miles from Winnipeg east to the eastern boundary of the western division. Then we have out in British Columbia two railways connecting the prairies with the Pacific
coast, one running to Vancouver and one running to Prince Rupert, and the prairie lines, as I understand it, have to carry the expenses of a tremendous amount of mileage that is not at all necessary for the needs of the prairie provinces so far as getting out to Fort William and Port Arthur and to the Pacific coast is concerned. We have also included in this region the unfinished Hudson Bay railway and a line to Prince Rupert that is practically valueless until more facilities are constructed at the coaisit. And then we have about 600 miles, about 300 miles each of the Canadian Northern and the Canadian National Railways, in the province of Ontario.
What line is it going west, out through the mountains, that is unnecessary?

So far as traffic is concerned the one to Prince Rupert is not necessary at the present time. It was built far ahead of the needs of the country and its maintenance is saddled on to the business that develops on the prairies.
In connection with the Superior division, the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) was at one time Chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners, and in his judgment in connection with the western rates case, speaking of the Lake Superior division, Canadian Railway cases, volume 17, "page 157, he said:
This division running as it does in great part through a wild and practically unsettled country, accompanied with great operating difficulties and with, of course, the lowest production of local tonnage per mile of line of any part of the C.P.R. nevertheless is shown to make good return.
