From that on there was an operating surplus, the amounts being as follows: April, $871,584; May, $964,436; June, $314,741; July, $765,742; August, $1,181,451; September, $1,125,167; October, $4,728,008; November, $4,094,048; and December, $2,760,625.
I have a statement here, but I am not going to read it because I do not want to take up too much time. It gives the total originating tonnage in the following commodities: Flour, potatoes, coal-anthracite, bituminous and lignite-coke, logs, pulpwood and lumber. I

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
have another statement with regard to originating tonnage of manufactured goods, but I shall not read that either to-night. I simply suggest that the statement I have given shows that the operating revenues-the gross revenues and the higher percentage of the net operating revenues-exists in proportion as the grain business increases in volume.
I want to say that is my answer to the statement that the western railways are not paying their share of operating costs and are not the asset they ought to be to this Dominion. It is also the answer to those who say that the Crowsnest pass rates on grain are unfair to the rest of Canada.
We have been told by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) that the Canadian Pacific finances the railway on its own credit, and that it is not in the same sense a charge against the Dominion. For my part I cannot see any difference in the Canadian Pacific spending $20,000,000 in constructing a railway and the Canadian National Railways acting likewise. There may be a technical difference but no difference actually as the people of Canada are going to pay for both. I have referred on a previous occasion to the statement of the Board of Railway Commissioners wherein they say that the Canadian Pacific is going to have such rates as will enable it to pay its dividends. Now, whether it is a case of this parliament undertaking to meet the obligations of the Canadian National Railway system or whether it is one of the obligations of the Canadian Pacific being guaranteed by parliament through the Board of Railway Commissioners, the result is the same-it is the people who pay the freight rates and in the last analysis there is practically no difference between them. So long as the order in question stands there is every reason why we in this parliament should demand every particle of information regarding the construction of Canadian Pacific branch lines as well as Canadian National branch lines. I have here a statement of the aid given to the Canadian Pacific Railway in the early days when it was making a struggle in this new country, but I shall not put it on Hansard, it would occupy too much time and too much space.
There is another matter I wish to mention, and it is not new either to the Minister of Railways or the hon. members of this House. I happen to represent a constituency that is one-half of the province of Alberta, and we have just about one-third as much railway mileage in that constituency as there is in the rest of the province of Alberta. I have
96i
been after the Minister of Railways for two sessions in order to get a railway built from somewhere near Grande Prairie, from McLennan or some other point, to the Canadian National Railway system. I am very much disappointed that the minister has not been able to get this line included in his branch line programme. I know there are difficulties as to certain parts of the railway. However, some sections have been definitely located, and I do not believe we are going to build another main line through the mountains for some years to come. I have been anxious to see this railway built so as to connect up the Peace river country and the coal area with the Canadian National system.
I should like to press upon the minister the desirability of doing something in that connection at the earliest possible moment.
I have here a copy of the Farm and Home published in Vancouver, British Columbia. It contains a few pictures, and one relates to a gentleman who went into the Grande Priarie country a number of years ago and invested $40,000 in farm land. Because a statement was issued some months ago that there would be no railway construction this year this gentleman has sold his forty-thousand-dollar, farm,-640 acres-as they call it, and is going to leave the country. Now, there have been those who have been advocating taking settlers out of that country, but to do that would cost more than to provide them with railway accommodation. Those settlers would be in a very favourable position if only the line in question were constructed.

I have no comment to
make on the latter part of the speech of the hon. member. I mean the part in which he referred to the real lack of any very great distinction, in so far as the effect on the taxpayer of Canada is concerned, between the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National Railway.

Would the right hon. gentleman permit a question? When my hon. friend referred to the last part of my statement I thought he was going to allude to the railway the construction of which I was urging. Now, would my right hon. friend give me his support in that enterprise?

I was supporting the
hon. member, and he did not seem to take to it very well.

I do not
recall that.

I hope my hon. friend
will not expect me to support everything at
C.N.It.-Branch Lines

once. I am considering the propositions one by one.
With the control now exercised by the government, or more directly by the Railway Commission, over rates, the other great railway system becomes a public service and a national corporation, compelling the people to take an almost equal interest in the cost of its operation and everything connected with its management, as in the case of the National Railways. There is a distinction but not a vast one. It is not a distinction that in earlier times prevailed. Nor do I quarrel very much with him in his later remarks. I am not making criticism at the present time either at what is being done. I know something of the difficulties that confront an administration of this kind. I want to make some comment on what the hon. member said in the first part of his speech. He was inclined to complain of the treatment received at the hands of this House of the western branch line legislation. I have been a member of this House for a considerable time, and whether as a Conservative or a Progressive, I certainly see no reason to complain of the treatment by this House of these western measures. I have never seen more generous treatment on the part of the House of any measures whatever.
Hon. members to his right, of some of whose words he complained, have supported virtually every one heartily. None have we opposed, and I do not think the hon. member would suggest that it was for political reasons, because if we can gain any of the seats that are to be served by these branch lines, well there would not be many in the Dominion, we would not possess.
I was not complaining about the support, but with regard to some of the statements made as to the political considerations.

I will come to that phase of it. I do not wish to pose as a great authority on railway traffic, but I think I know enough about it to say that the problem is not quite so simple as it appears to be in the mind of the hon. member. He states that the returns brought down by the government as respects the National Railways in the Maritime provinces, or rather in the Atlantic division, show a loss of some $5,000,000 on operation. In the western provinces-that is the western division from Armstrong and Fort William westward-the returns show a loss of some $2,000,000, and in the central provinces, outside entirely of the more western Grand Trunk route, a profit of some $18,000,000. These figures are correct. In the western Grand Trunk territory I believe a profit of

some $8,000,000 besides was claimed. These are the figures brought down by the government. I must emphatically say that a closer investigation of the returns makes it entirely impossible for me to understand the figures. I do not think they are correct, but I think proportionately they are about correct as between the different divisions. I do not think there have been those returns as respects what ought to be called operation and as respects everything that ought to be included in operation. I do not think those figures can be sustained at all, but that point does not arise at the moment. I have no doubt the proportions are correct. But the hon. gentleman says, "You cannot claim that you are losing money in the West and that it is our fault, because we have unnecessary mileage there in the way of far western outlets. We have three far western outlets to the Pacific, and these are more than are necessary." On being questioned to be specific, he admitted very frankly and perfectly correctly that the unnecessary one for the purpose of western outlet is the Grand Trunk Pacific. That may be true, and I believe it is, but we are dealing now with the relative burden, and it is equally true-far more than true-of the central division. In the central division, if the Transcontinental did not carry freight that would otherwise go by the more direct route into the populated part of central Canada, the loss on it would be simply terrific. The unnecessary mileage in the centre bears down as heavily there as the unnecessary mileage in the West, and the same can be said of the Maritime provinces. On the same principle you could not tax any division with its loss; but the trouble is that we have to tax them and we have got to sustain the road, so that the hon. gentleman's argument falls down. Then he comes to the rescue from another angle, and he says it is the grain crop of the West that pays. He says, "That is the crop that pays, so that we are paying sufficient." I do not say that we are not paying sufficient. There is no one who would be more anxious than I to get the rate lower if we could do so. Certainly every cent we take off is saved to the producer, and there should be nothing in the world left undone that would drive down lower and lower the western carriage freights, and especially the rate on grain. But to say that everything is fair to-day. or that rates have been too high, and to base that assertion cm the argument of the hon. member is fallacious. He says, "Take the returns month by month, and you will find

that when the grain crop comes in those foundation at all, and to-day I am sorry to gross returns increase." Yes, the proportion say this prejudice exists in a measure that I of profit increases, but what in the world for one as a Canadian deplore, would you expect? That is when the busi- j^r FORKE: Did the hon. gentleman read ness is done. These are the months in which the gpgggh lately by the vice-president of the the business is carried on. line, the more dense the traffic, unquestionably the greater the profit. For example, if we could ship grain out of the West, every month as fast as we ship it out in October, we could afford a much lower rate on grain. The grain rate would go away down, but it is just because it is of a seasonal character that we cannot afford to put the rate down. There has to be maintenance the year round in order to take care of this great rush of traffic in the two or three months.	[DOT]
Mr. Lanigan stated last year before the Railway committee that the cars were not idle during the summer. I have the quotation here.

I would require to see the words and the context in order to discuss that. We all know that the great rush of traffic is confined to two or three months. There could not possibly be the same equalization during the rest of the year. I have talked to railway men both on the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railway, and I know that there are times, especially in the cold weather, during which all grain is carried at a loss, and necessarily so. But on the contrary, as against that, there is a profit during the rush season, and the whole thing has to be levelled up on that basis. The return has to be fixed. One could approach the matter from several other angles as well. I do not think I am breaking any confidence when I say that the claim as to loss is not confined to the one railway. The other railway still claims that grain had been carried from the province of Alberta throughout the entire year at a loss. We want to get things down to a common basis and to know what we are doing. We want to be fair to every part of Canada, but it seems to me that these returns do indicate that the West at least has no reason to complain and that there is no reason in the world to say to parliament, "You have been unjust to us". I come from western Canada, and I think I am as much a western man as the hon. member, but I say that hon. members have gone through that country, have complained of the treatment of eastern Canada, and have raised prejudices against eastern Canada and against this parliament without the slightest
I have not read it, but I have read speeches of eastern men that are equally to be deplored.
I do not think you can beat it.
Perhaps not, but hon. gentlemen should take care that they do not provoke it, and if there are those who are guilty of that offence-
Not guilty.
-it is hon. gentlemen to my left. They are not so guilty in this House as they are out in western Canada.
That is not fair, now.

If it is not fair, I am
the one that knows it.

Does the right hon.
member remember the speech which he himself made in the last election campaign about a certain part of Canada being more loyal than some other parts?
I do not remember because it was never made. That exists only in the imagination of my hon. friend, or perhaps it was produced by the imaginative pen of some critical foe.
Did he ever read in the papers a report to that effect?

I have read some very
strange reports, even reports that represent themselves to be statements by hon. members to my left. All I want to say is that nothing to justify in the faintest possible respect the statement which the hon. member has attributed to me from the press was ever uttered by myself. He will find, as he goes on in public life, that perhaps he will suffer from some of this kind of thing himself. All I rose to say was this, that the case is not established that there is too high a rate merely by showing that you make a profit during the heavy traffic on grain. Not at all. It is, the hon. member thinks?
I do.

I am afraid my hon.
friend will have great difficulty in convincing any who have to do with this subject and
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

who have made it the study of their lives. I wonder how hon. members would like to have imposed on them and their constituents rates that are imposed to-day on their competitors to the south for the carriage of grain. I fancy that is about what would result if any of this talk that we sometimes hear about secession eventuates in fact. I do not myself see anything else that could result, and as one who has given some study to this matter, I heard yesterday morning that the rates to the south that are there borne by the producers of grain-
What about grain for export?

In so far as they have to be borne for the carrying of export grain, their proportion is necessarily much smaller. Those rates if applied to western Canada would mean an increase of twenty-two to twenty-five, or possibly thirty million dollars in the carriage of a crop equal to the crop of last year.

Are the
grain rates across the line not very largely domestic?
Yes, they are.

How do
they compare with British Columbia rates?

I wish they were domestic here. They will never be domestic here if hon. gentlemen to my left have their way. In so far as they are comparable with ours, they are so much higher that, if applied to our railways, they would impose a burden on the West of from twenty-five to thirty million dollars a year.

It was not my intention to take any part in this debate on railway extension nor would I have done so had the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Kennedy) not made some remarks in connection with the railroad into the Peace river country. When he made that statement in connection with the extension from the Grand Trunk Pacific starting at Brule to Grande Prairie, he failed to tell the committee that Grande Prairie has a railroad and elevators at the present time built by the Alberta government at the request of the people in that district, a railroad that costs the Alberta government in the neighbourhood of a million and a half dollars a year.
My reason for not intending to say anything on this subject just now was that that extension is under consideration by the Railway Board. Another extension is under con-
[Mr. Meighen.I
sideration as well, an extension from Prince George into the Peace river block where this government owns 3,500,000 acres of land. The Alberta side of the Peace river country has a railroad extending from Edmonton to McLennan, another line that runs north and crosses the Peace river, one that runs east to Spirit river and another that runs down to Grande Prairie. There is practically a network of railways, and still they want this government to build another line from Brule into that section to take the freight that justly belongs to the Edmonton railroad for the benefit of the Canadian National road. On the other hand if an extension were built from Prince George into the Peace river country it would traverse a country of good agricultural land where there is no railway, where the people have no transportation not even by a road, and where the country is equally as good as that at Grande Prairie.

It is quite true, as the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride) says, that there is a railway into Grande Prairie and one to the north into the Peace river. That road was built with the intention at some time of connecting it with the Canadian National, and we 9 p.m. want to complete that connection at what we consider the best point and in the best way. It does not matter where this line is built, feeders will have to be built to the various parts of the Peace river country. Those will have to be developed no matter whether the line goes west through the mountains or south. The district of Pouce Coupe in the Peace river block will have to be served by a railway, but I believe this is the best method of providing railway facilities for the whole country, and I am advocating it for that reason.

Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:

C .N.R.-Branch Lines
Resolved, That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide for the construction of a Canadian National Railway line from a point on the Victoria Beach subdivision of the Canadian Northern Railway near East Selkirk, in an easterly and then in a northeasterly direction, to Pine Falls in the province of Manitoba; estimated mileage including existing grading, 44 miles; estimated cost, $1,100,000.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

The following is the
memorandum I have concerning this line:
Pine Falls-Mile 0-44.	Cost
Proposed in 1924-44 miles grade	$374,000
Proposed in 1925-44 miles track and ballast. 726,000

This branch as proposed will be 44 miles long leaving the Victoria Beach Subdivision near East Selkirk and terminating on the Winnipeg river near the Fort Alexander Indian Reserve. In 1924 it is proposed to do the grading of the 44 miles and in 1925 to lay the track thereon at an estimated cost of $726,000.
The construction of this line is conditional on a paper mill being built at Pine Falls.
One of the purpQses of this branch is to serve a pulp and paper plant to be built on the Winnipeg river at Pine Falls. It will also serve a good agricultural country on the way besides shortening the route into the mining district now developing north of the Winnipeg river. The immediate terminus will be near a good crossing of the river so as to make it possible to readily extend this line when necessary.
When complete the proposed pulp and paper plant would supply immediately about 1,500 cars per year of their product, which will steadily grow with the expansion of this industry, besides considerable inbound freight of merchandise and other supplies. The local farm territory would also furnish considerable outbound business. The freight to and from the pulp and paper plant would not only be handled over this branch but would extend for distribution over the company's line to various points, therefore mean considerable long haul traffic to the railway.
I have been told that the construction of the paper mill referred to in the foregoing memorandum has begun, but I am not sure of that. Originally it was intended to build this line directly through the shortest route to the pulp and paper mill but the board after consideration concluded that the line should be extended, in the way set forth in the memorandum, to serve not only the pulp and paper mill but a good farming country as well.

Has the government,
through the Department of the Interior, cruised or inspected the area carefully enough to see whether there is probability of any great amount of freight for any considerable length of time even if the mill is built? It is just possible that we might find ourselves with the railway in years to come with no pulp mill erected nor any lumber being used. That is the first question. In the second place, what is the actual condition of affairs in regard to the pulpwood? I understand that these are
Mr. J. D. McArthur's interests. Has he managed to finance the business, and if so what concessions were made him?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: So far as I know he has not been able yet to finance the undertaking. One of the difficulties is that in the area in which the mill is located there is only a possible supply of 800,000 cords of pulpwood, and that largely on a concession that was granted to him in the first instance. That, as a result of cruises that have been made, is the most recent information that I have from the McArthur interests in connection with the pulp and paper mill.

I do not want to offer any objection to this branch line, but inasmuch as references have been made to the alleged opposition of eastern members to western development, some suggestion having been made as to main lines that were not being used to great advantage, and comparisons having been drawn as between the gross revenue of the western section and that of the Atlantic region, I think I ought to tell the committee that the Transcontinental from Levis into Moncton, part of the line between Monk and Moncton being part and parcel of the Atlantic region, is not securing the traffic which it was intended to carry. For this reason the Atlantic region is unable to meet expenses. I should like to ask the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) a question regarding railway development in the county of Kent. The statement has been made that a branch line will be constructed between Buctouche and Richibucto which is a section of the country that needs railway facilities, not only to accommodate the people on the line but also to move agricultural produce and the products of the fisheries and the lumber industry between Richibucto and Buctouche as feeders to the main line of the Canadian National Railways. Inasmuch as members of the government have already expressed themselves in favour of that construction, my constituents have a right to know whether the government has come to any decision in the matter. I understand that the proposed line was very favourably reported upon by the engineers who were in charge of the work in 1919-20. It is true that in 1920 the then president of the Canadian National Railways, in view of the financial crisis that faced the country at that time and also of the fact that the government of the day was not recommending the construction of new branch lines, did not implement the report of the engineers. And in 1923 the present president of the Canadian National Railways, without making
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

any investigation, assumed that that section of the province had sufficient accommodation by water, which is not the case in one sense, since water facilities from Richibucto or St. Louis to St. John are out of the question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I fear the remarks of the hon. member are hardly relevant to the question under consideration. He is making a detailed speech concerning a matter that is far removed from the subject of the resolution.

If I am guilty of any transgression, Mr. Chairman, my offence is only in keeping with that of my hon. friend from West Edmonton, who a short while ago was discussing a branch line that had nothing to do with the resolution then before the Chair.

I am glad my hon. friend is so confiding. If he will look up Hansard in the years he has mentioned he will find that provision was made for twenty lines in 1919-20, which did not include the one he is advocating. However, that is a matter of memory or of research on his part. The transportation question in Rent county is one that has been before all governments, but up to the present the line my hon. friend suggests has not been constructed. There is a Kent Northern line, with a mileage of about 27 miles, owned by a private company, and while the matter has been before one or two governments the fact is that the people of Kent county themselves are not in agreement as to what should be done, whether the Kent Northern line should be taken over and rehabilitated or whether the branch line to which my hon. friend refers should be constructed. There has been a good deal of discussion and correspondence from the point of view of both these proposals. I had an interview with the gentleman who was acting for the Kent Northern, and while I thought the property was not a very valuable one I was considering with him the suggestion of making a proposal to parliament concerning it. However, we did not come to any terms, and these matters will all have to be considered. We can do only so many things at a time, and I can assure my hon. friend that the fact that he is here will not make a bit of difference, will not prejudice the investigation of the railway situation in Kent county.
The minister should not repudiate his colleague in that way. He must have forgotten what the Secretary of State (Mr. Copp) said in the county itself.

As my right hon. friend
knows, we read many things in newspapers with regard to what people are supposed to have said. However, I am speaking at present for the Minister of Railways and pointing out the difficulties that have been met with in the past in the matter of doing something for the county of Kent.
My right hon. friend referred to something I had said. I do not know just what he refers to-
I have the words here.
Taken from what?

I read it in the debate
on the Address. The hon. member did not object then.

Well, I take my own time to object to it. What my right hon. friend quoted shortly after the opening of parliament was not what I said in the county of Kent; it was absolutely incorrect. My right hon. friend was, I suppose, misinformed in regard to that just as he has been misinformed in regard to many other matters in connection with his public career. I had the extreme pleasure of being in the county of Kent during the election that was held there, and I referred to transportation matters in a number of addresses I made in the county. I should have thought that the hon. member for Kent would have been quite satisfied with the result of the election without misrepresenting myself or any person else in regard to what had been said. I made no such statement as was reported in the Moncton Times in regard to the building of a railway or the taking over of a railway by the government. I mentioned a railway the construction of which had been talked about', from the town of Buctouche to Richibucto, a matter that had been before the public for a number of years and in connection with which suggestions had been made.
I told the people decidedly and emphatically in the course of a number of addresses I made that I had not come there to promise the building of a railway because it took considerable time to give consideration to the building of any portion of a railway, even of short mileage.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think it is my duty to tell the hon. member that this discussion has continued to be out of order through several courses.

I think, Mr. Chairman, that I should be given the same privilege as that extended to the member for Kent in discussing this matter, particularly in view of the fact

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
that a promise on behalf of the government to build a railway in that section has been attributed to me. I want to say to you, Mr. Chairman, to my hon. friend from the county of Kent and to the right hon. leader of the opposition, that I made no such promise in regard to the building of a railway or any portion of railway mileage in the county of Kent. What results may come from negotiations that have been proceeding between myself, the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) and the representatives of the owners of the Kent Northern railway, remains to be seen. The matter has been under negotiation for some time. I quite agree with the member for Kent that this transportation question should be given consideration and I sincerely trust that before very long, in spite of the fact that it is he who is here representing that county, it may be considered favourably.

The hon. member's
memory is very short. Nobody ever alleged in this House that he promised a railway to the county of Kent. That was never alleged by me in my address. I read distinctly what I attributed to him, and it did not promise a railway. It was the hon. member's habit to be conditional in his intimations; everything depended. I hope the committee will bear with me while I quote the words he used, so that no one will go away with a misunderstanding. They were given to me as having been taken down verbatim. I do not think the paper from which I took them was the one to which he. refers, nor do I think that the hon. member, if he will listen to the words exactly, will undertake to deny them. His words were these:
Now, I want to ask you in all fairness, who will be your representative? Who will be more apt to get a more reasonable and fair consideration for you,-
The hon. member must recognize that the language is characteristic.
-Doucet, the Conservative candidate, or Bourgeois? It is to your very great advantage, and I believe it is your bounden duty, if you want better railway facilities for this part of Kent, to elect Mr. Bourgeois, who will co-operate with me and my colleagues to give the people of this county what they deserve and what they want.
I never made such a statement in the county of Kent, irrespective of where my right hon. friend got his information.

Mr. Chairman, may I
break up this little family affair?
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Graham thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 62, respecting the construction of a Canadian National Railway line to Pine Falls in the province of Manitoba.
Motion agreed to, bill read the first ahd second times and refered to the select standing committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines.

I have no desire to oppose this if the minister has evidence that it will pay. Will the minister say that in his belief this road will pay the cost of operation, to say nothing of interest on construction?

I am not in a position
to say that. In the construction of branch lines throughout the Dominion it is very difficult to outline a profit at the very beginning, but the building of a branch line into a territory where business is expanding develops business ,to a point where it will eventually pay, and this particular line will be a great accommodation to the people of this town as it will enable them to load their fish and freight at their own town instead of having to haul it four miles each way.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Graham thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 63, respecting the construction of a Canadian National Railway line between Lockeport station and the town of Lockeport, in the province of Nova Scotia.
Motion agreed to, bill read the first and second times, and referred to the select standing committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN QUEBEC RAILWAY-CHINA CLAY BRANCH EXTENSION

speechtext:
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide for the construction of a Canadian National (Mr. Graham.]
Railway line, being an extension of the China Clay branch of the Canadian Northern Quebec Railway to the town of St. Remi d'Amherst, in the province of Quebec; estimated mileage including existing grading, 2 miles; estimated cost, $105,000.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN QUEBEC RAILWAY-CHINA CLAY BRANCH EXTENSION
speechtext:
The resolution explains
itself. It is to provide for an extension of a small line of railway two miles into the town of St. Remi d'Amherst. With reference to the traffic, the deputy minister received a letter a day or so ago from the Singer Manufacturing Company, which I think would be of interest:
The Singer Manufacturing Company Factory No. 5 -St. Johns, P.Q., Canada,
76-77 Banque Nationale Building, Rideau Street, Ottawa, Ont.
Ottawa, March 19th, 1924. -
Mr. G. A. Bell,
Deputy Minister,
Department of Railways and Canals,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir:
In regard to proposed extension of the Canadian National Railway, from China Clay to St. Remi d'Amherst, and which was included with other extensions in one bill introduced in the Dominion parliament at the last session, and finally rejected en bloc by the Senate, we understand that your department this session is again asking parliament to sanction the construction of this extension, which, if judged on its own merits, there is no doubt but that the estimate would be passed.
2.	The service as it now exists at China Clay is very bad, the siding is we understand a private one, subject to an extra charge to shippers, limited to four or five cars and very hard to approach.
3.	The building of this short extension of 2$ miles will greatly facilitate the people in that part of the country doing business with your Company, it would also encourage them to deliver for shipment an increased tonnage.

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
4.	Owing to having acquired all the standing timber on government lands lying west of the Rouge watershed, some 500 square miles, we are very much interested that your company provide shipping facilities at St. Remi. This season we have several small mills manufacturing some 2,000,000 feet of lumber, amounting to about 150 carloads, this will be available for shipment over the C.N.R. from St. Remi, providing a suitable service is given. During the twelve months ending July 31st, 1923, there were 343 carioads shipped locally from China Clay, and on which the shippers, we understand, had to pay a private siding charge of $3 per car. In the past this company has received good service from the C.X.R. in connection with freight movements, and we trust that they will maintain their record at St. Remi.
Yours very truly,
TFE/B The Singer Manufacturing Company,
T. F. Elinitt.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN QUEBEC RAILWAY-CHINA CLAY BRANCH EXTENSION
speechtext:
I wish, Sir, to make a few remarks with regard to this resolution authorizing the construction of two miles only of railway. Comparing this resolution with similar ones which we have adopted, we notice that it will be the shortest branch line, and yet, it is one of the most important. It is the last resolution with reference to branch lines, and I must remark that in my opinion, it is the most necessary.
These two miles of railway will cost $105,000 and are an absolute necessity for the people of my county. This was acknowledged within the last years and already the companj'' of the River Rouge had made an attempt to build these two miles so as to connect the line of the Canadian Northern from Quebec to the village 'of St. Remi d'Amherst. The said two miles only extend the present existing line as far as the village of St. Remi d'Amherst. It is actually not a new branch, but rather the completion of one of the most important railways and certainly the most useful for this region. The proof that these two miles are important, as just mentioned, is that there was an attempt during the last years, to connect the branch line of the Monfort Railway to the village of St. Remi d'Amherst. This region andl its surroundings are most important from the standpoint of farming, industry and mining. There exists in these parts numerous parishes settled since a great number of years, parishes that are thickly populated and that are at
some distance from railways. It is true that the Canadian Northern line, at present the Canadian National, extends towards this region; however, there has never been up to the present a passenger service anywhere near the region of St. Remi d'Amherst and the surrounding country. The terminus of the Canadian Northern, at present the Canadian National Railways, has always been at Huber-deau, and passenger trains only run on this line, to the village of Huberdeau.
However, about ten years ago, eight miles of railway were constructed, extending towards the county of Labelle. The latter line was only used for freight and especially for the operation of the Canadian China Clay mine, a well developed and prosperous porcelain industry, which was being worked at that time. However, although the eight miles of line are built, there is practically no freight service from St. Remi d'Amherst and surroundings, and further there is no passenger service from China Clay to Huberdeau or on -the remainder of the branch line of the Canadian National Railways. Now, by the construction of these two miles of line to the village of St. Remi d'Amherst, you will practically put into operation ten miles of railway, in a district which is not at present served by any railway. In that territory, where are to be seen quite a number of parishes, having a prosperous farming population, there are no railways to be found along a considerable portion of it. The nearest railway is the Canadian Pacific, which follows the course of the Ottawa river; it is located at a distance of from 25 to 30 miles from St. Remi d'Amherst. To the north, the distance is 20 to 25 miles in order to reach the branch line of the Canadian Pacific, which starts at Montreal and extends to the regions of Mont Laurier. It is, therefore, absolutely necessary that this district be provided with a railway.
I have already, on many occasions, expounded the excellent reasons which militate in favour of these two miles extension. I do not wish this evening, to go over the ground again; I shall just draw the attention of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) to a few facts. In case there should be a sale of this branch line to the Canadian Pacific Railway-a sale which I do not desire, on the contrary, for I have already had occasion to protest-for reasons which I am far from admitting are well founded, although the government might consider that they are in the public interest, if the government decided to sell this branch line to the Canadian Pacific Railway, I would request that said sale take
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

place only on the well understood condition that the construction of these two miles of railway be carried! out, so as to complete the branch line and make it profitable for the company operating it, and especially to afford to the central part of the county of Labelle, the advantage of possessing a railway which would be of service to it.
Mr. FAFARD (Translation) Will the hon. member allow me to ask a question? Are the electors of the county of Labelle in favour of this branch line?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN QUEBEC RAILWAY-CHINA CLAY BRANCH EXTENSION
speechtext:
Certainly,
Sir, the electors of the county of Labelle are favourable to such a project, and I think that the aim of the hon. member's question, is to press me to further state with more emphasis that this branch line is necessary to the county of Labelle and that my constituents would gladly endorse its construction. A last advice which I shall give to the Minister of Railways regarding this extension of two miles, is this: There is, along these two miles, works which have already been carried out by the company of River Rouge. The latter, incorporated by authority of a prominent statute and having as its object the construction of a railway line along a distance of about 80 miles, from Grenville towards the northern part of the county of Labelle, this company had attempted to construct two miles of railway along the line to be built and had consequently started work at a place known as the Canadian China Clay, extending as far as the village of St. Remi d'Amherst. I am aware that the Department of Railways could take no account of the work done previously by the River Rouge Railway Company, however, if it is possible for the Department of Railways to purchase on fair terms the improvements already carried out by said company, I would certainly approve of the department making the necessary advances so as to acquire such assets. These consist primarily in the location of the line, also, I think, in certain rights of way secured on part of those two miles and the grading of the roadbed. Consequently, the work done would be useful to the Department of Railways when constructing the said extension of two miles and would help to complete the work in the shortest time possible. Naturally, on acquiring these works the department could also stipulate that the money be not paid to the representatives of the River Rouge unless the farmers and labourers of St. Remi d'Amherst and the country around1 Labelle are paid for their claims in connection with the construction work done on said two miles of railway. A few years ago when this

work was undertaken by the River Rouge company, a number of people from St. Remi d'Amiherst and surrounding villages were employed by the company. They have certain claims against this company for wages and material supplied. The River Rouge company stopped the work and it seems did not settle all the legitimate claims of these people. It would therefore, be only fair that in the purchase which the department may make of the road, it should hold back a sufficient amount to settle all these people's claims.
One last remark, Sir, I entirely approve of this resolution as it provides for the construction of two miles of railway which are most important in a region that certainly deserves the government's consideration because these parts are completely deprived of means of communication. It is a vast farming district, very rich in natural resources, and these two miles of railway will be of great advantage, not only to this region but also to the National Railways for it will be one of the most paying branch lines of this road.
Resolution reported, read1 the second time and concurred in. Mr. Graham: thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 64, respecting the construction of a Canadian National Railway line from the end1 of the China Clay branch to St. Remi d'Amherst in the province of Quebec.
Motion agreed to, bill read the first and second times and referred to the select standing committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines.

The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Marcil (Bonaventure) in the chair.
Cold storage warehouses, $30,000.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
The reduction in this item is
accounted for by the fact that there has been much less demand during the last two or three years for cold storage, and that we are desirous of keeping our estimates down. The sum of $30,000 will, I think, take care of all the contracts we have entered into with the various plants throughout Canada. There is a plant at Sydney, Cape Breton, that has been under construction for several years. I had the opportunity of visiting this very excellent plant last summer. I think it is almost ready for business now. It is a well finished and well insulated building. We have another one in Quebec and another one in Prince Edward Island. These are the three we have under contract, and this sum we think will take

Supply-Agriculture
care of them. In the meantime we are not taking any more under contract for the present. These are established under the terms of the old Cold Storage Act.

Do these cold storage
plants put up at the cost of the government pay their way? If some of them do not pay their way, would the minister tell the House which ones pay and which do not?

I think possibly the hon. member who asks the question was not in the House last year when we went over this question very thoroughly. The government does not put up these plants. Under the terms of the Cold Storage Act, the government subsidizes them to the extent of 30 per cent of the cost of construction. This $30,000 is spread over four or five payments at different times, based upon progress estimates. After the subsidy is all paid we have the supervision of these plants. Whether they pay or not is up to the people operating them. This subsidy was originally designed with the idea of assisting them to become established. While cold storage is required in Canada, the public itself, until quite recently has not been educated, shall we say, or developed to the importance of cold storage. The result was that up to the time of the war the demand was comparatively limited. During the war there was a tremendous demand for cold storage on account of the necessity for keeping a large quantity of produce on hand for shipment. Since the war the demand has fallen off, with the result that a great many of these plants throughout Canada find it difficult sledding to make ends meet. I would not like to say that none of them pay, but they have a hard time. People are not demanding space. They feel like economizing and not using the space.

Is the department under any
obligation to repair, or is this vote for original construction?
Original construction.
No obligation to repair?
No.

The department has three
original plants now.
Yes.

Did the minister state where
they were?

I did not quite
understand the question. The three I have mentioned are under contract but there are
some thirty altogether. One is located at Prince Rupert, and others scattered through Canada right down to Halifax.

I am not familiar with the
terms of the act. Are the proceedings leading to this subsidy initiated by private enterprise, or how?

Yes. We are just proceeding under the provisions of the act. The bill went through last year and my hon. friend from Parkdale (Mr. Spence) will remember that he was not very uproarious about supporting it. The bill did not get past the other Chamber, and the result is that we are operating under the old act that does not make any reservations or restrictions about the kind of cold storage, whether they are municipal or private or co-operative or what they are. The plant at Sydney is a' private one; the one on Prince Edward Island is private and the one at Quebec city is cooperative.

The minister told us a few moments ago that these are not under the control of the government. Under whose control is the cold storage at Montreal at the harbour? I was under the impression that that was under government control.
The cold storage at Montreal is under the harbour board just the same as the elevators.
It is government owned?

Yes. It is under
the administration of the Haibour Board of Montreal. They own and administer it just the same as they do the elevators there. I know that within nine months of its opening, 75 per cent of the space was taken. I have not the figures here, but if it is patronised now as well as it was the first year, it is doing pretty well.
Has the minister received any representations from the Okanagan and Salmon river country regarding cold storage, pre-cooling plants for fruit?

Yes, we had representations by a deputation. Mr. Mutrie and Mr. Bulman were here after the New Year, and while we cannot anticipate the supplementary estimates too much, there is nothing in this item for that and possibly there may be something in the supplementaries with regard to it. Last year we gave two grants for pre-cooling institutions, one lat Grimsby and one at New Westminster. The one at Grimsby is doing excellent work for the fruit producers of that district. As regards
Supply-Agriculture

the one at New Westminster the parties to whom we expected to make .the subsidy did not comply with the conditions and the subsidy was not paid out. At Okanagan, Salmon Arm and at one or two other places, I am pretty well convinced that if we can raise the money it would be a good investment to assist the fruit growers in some measure, on about the same basis as this, namely 30 per cent, and put pre-cooling plants in their fruit packing establishments. They have the buildings, and all that has to be done is to insulate the necessary space properly. With the tremendous rush of fruit on the market, every medium should be taken advantage of to dispose of the fruit at that season, whether it be by pre-cooling, refrigerating, drying or selling the fruit fresh, so that every method of taking care of the glut at that time should receive our consideration.

I am glad to hear
the minister intimate that there is some hope in the supplementary estimates of doing something for that district.

I am not making
a definite promise.

I suppose the minister understands that it makes all the difference in the world as regards the shipment of apples to a foreign market if they are precooled first. I should like to ask a question about dehydrating plants, although I understand that comes under another item. One was started at Penticton last year and it was burned down. I noticed in the store windows a few weeks ago some new wonderful exhibits of apples put up in cartons by the department here, and I believe a great industry could be worked up in our country if something is done to encourage it.

We have an item
further down for dehydration:
For experiments in the dehydration of fruits and vegetables, $15,000.
The amount last year was $10,500. I do not know whether we have quite decided to rebuild in the same place or not, but it is our intention to rebuild so as to serve that territory. In view of the' large quantity of dried fruit that we import into this country and the large quantity of fresh fruit that becomes a glut on our market at harvest time, there is no reason in the world why a great deal of the fresh fruit that we find it impossible to sell should not be converted into the dried fruit of which we are importing so much.
I Mr. Motherwell.]

Has the minister
placed on the market any of the product that has been put out by the department at Ottawa?

Yes, it is on the
market now.

It is a well known fact
that the cold storage at Montreal has lost a great deal of money in the last number of years. Is it possible that the government does not lose some of that when it is subsidizing cold storages? The minister stated that it is paying well. I understand that it is not paying at all, and we want to get the facts.

I told the committee that that did not come under this item. That comes under the Minister of Marine and Pisheries (Mr. Cardin). The estimate is submitted: by the harbour board. I was merely saying that if we may judge from the space that is occupied, it ought to be doing fairly well. I have not been there for a year.

It does not come under this
item ?

No. It does not
come under my administration.

A few minutes ago an hon. member asked a question about the cold storage plant, and the minister said that he was not particularly interested; that it was a private concern. Are we not particularly interested to the extent of 30 per cent? We should want to see these plants pay rather than make a failure of their business.
Mr, MOTHERWELL:	My hon. friend is
straining a little bit.

No, I am pretty well
posted on this job.

I do not doubt
that, but the subsidies, as a rule, are paid before you can tell whether they are going to be paying concerns or not. WTe take every precaution to begin with to see that they are placed in an area where they are likely to pay, to see that all the conditions of the contract are complied with. When the regulations and the law are complied with, we pay over the subsidy at some four or five different periods according to the terms laid down in the regulations. After that we are concerned with everything, but we have no responsibility.

Supply-A griculture

But you have, you have
given them so much money.

Yes, we have that
money there, and it was given as a subsidy without many strings to it. I should not say that such a plant is under our control; it is under our inspection, and the rates are only in a measure under our control. In last year's bill we had provision for subsequent control; the question was discussed for a long time in the Agricultural committee, and it was felt that after the last subsidy was paid there was very little control. The bill of last year provided for specific control even after the subsidies were paid; but that bill did not go through, and the result is that we are under the old act. There is some control but not the amount that some people think we should have.

I am not knocking precooling plants; I think they are an absolute necessity at points like those that have been mentioned; but I do not think
10 p.m. the minister should encourage private individuals to go into the cold storage business if he does not think they are going to make it pay, because people have lost thousands, yes, millions of dollars in building cold storage plants on account of having been encouraged by the government to go into that business. If the minister has not a real demand from somebody who knows something about the cold storage business, he should discourage or, perhaps, to put the matter more mildly, not encourage private individuals to go into the cold storage business.

We have nearly
cut the vote in two, keeping just enough to carry out the contracts already entered into, and we are not entering upon any new ones. The plant at Sydney will take the greater part of the money. It is about five years now since the preliminaries were begun in connection with the work at Sydney, the matter having had its inception before this government came in at all. We had nothing to do with it in the early stages, our duty now being simply to pay the subsidy. As regards the other two, the one in Quebec city is operated in conjunction with the Farmers' Co-operative Association of that province, while the one in Prince Edward Island involves only a small expenditure of $6,000. We are disposed to take my hon. friend's advice and I can assure him that we shall not enter into any new contracts under present circumstances.

So long as the act is ip force, any private enterprise or any municipality can erect a cold storage building and call upon' the department to provide the subsidy mentioned in the act. While that legislation stands I do not see that the department can help paying the 30 per cent.

We have of course the option of refusing it if we think there is ample cold storage facility already available. We do not want to repeal the act because we may find it desirable at some time to take advantage of its provisions when money is more plentiful. There has not been sufficiently satisfactory control over these institutions after the subsidy has been paid, and although we made provision last year to meet this difficulty the act did not pass the Senate, so that we are in the same position that we held before. The whole business is petering out now to such an extent that we do not think it advisable to amend the act.
Does the department control the cold storage plants by regulation from the standpoint of sanitation, efficiency and so forth?
Yes.
To what extent?

We have power by statute to make regulations but it is questionable whether that power can be legally exercised. For example, we can apply regulations, say, in Prince Rupert to control rates and to govern the period of time that goods shall remain in cold storage, and so on. But it is very questionable whether federal control in that direction can be exercised. At least that is the advice we have received. The regulations apply, for instance, to such questions as the authorized capital, the subscribed capital, and the rates for storage, which, as originally approved by the Governor in Council, shall not be increased without further approval by the same authority. There is also a regulation in regard to owners entering into special contracts with customers for the maintenance of temperatures other than those specifically provided for.

If unsanitary conditions
prevail, or if foodstuffs are destroyed, does the Department of Agriculture, or the Department of Health, exercise jurisdiction?

I think the municipal law would apply in that case. We have had instances of the kind in Winnipeg and Regina and if I remember rightly the muni-
Supply-Agriculture

cipal health authorities ordered the destruction of the foodstuffs.

I understand that the department has carried out a number of experiments with regard to the various temperatures maintained in the shipment of fruit in refrigerator cars. What progress has been made in that respect?

In the shipment of fruit from Grimsby west large quantities of ice are used in the chilling of cars, and I believe that it has been decided to recommend the construction of some special cars for the purposes of refrigeration.

Item agreed to.
Fruit, $182,000.

What are the details of this
item?
This vote is largely consumed in inspection work and marketing.

Was it all expended
last year?

I think so. It is
well to have a little leeway, but we do not exceed the vote.

What proportion of the vote
is used in salaries of inspectors and other officers?

Between 80 and 90 per cent. Apart from the vote for compensation under "Health of Animals", the fair grants and cold storage, practically the whole body of the agricultural vote is used in salaries for inspection, education, or other work of that nature. The salaries amount to about 85 per cent.

Have there been any
complaints in regard to the inspection of fruit in British Columbia?

We have not had
any reports of complaints. We shall be very glad to hear any.

I am glad to hear
that. I quite believe that the reason you have not heard any complaints is that the work is carried out in a very excellent manner. I have no doubt that the chief inspector there, Mr. Clarke, is about as competent a man as the department could find if they searched Canada from coast to coast. As one who is very thoroughly conversant with the situation out there, I am very glad to bear that testimony.

That is gratifying. We do not get very much of that and I suppose I should express my appreciation of it. My hon. friend will be interested in the investigational work conducted by the experimental farm out there in connection with the Jonathan apple, which in the last few years has developed a disease which has the effect of darkening the apple and breaking it down. The experimental farm carried out experiments in co-operation with the growers with a view to finding out something about this disease; they had the idea that it had something to do with the time that the apple was harvested. After experiments over some eight or nine different periods, starting with the earlier periods and following along later into the season, it was found that up to about the sixth period the apples kept well but when left on the tree after that they broke down. The experts have been unable to define exactly what the disease is, but it has been found to be associated with the time of harvesting, and the solution is to harvest the apple early.

Would there not be
some trouble in regard to grading if the apple was taken so early as to preclude danger from this disease?
No, you can have it sufficiently mature to grade and to keep, but it must not remain too long on the tree. That is a matter of judgment.

Has the department
any reports concerning a similar rot in McIntosh Red apples?

No, It has been
confined almost entirely to the Jonathan apple.
Is there any marked improvement this year in the keeping qualities of the Jonathan apple.

Oh yes. A year
ago we were entirely in the dark.

You claim now to have
discovered the cause for the rot?

Yes, and, by the
way, that discovery can be attributed to the experimental farms.

About what amount of early
soft fruits and vegetables are imported from the United States?

Is my hon. friend suggesting that a good many of them come in? Yes, a lot of fruit and vegetables come in from the south before ours are ripe. Has my hon. friend any suggestion as to how we

Supply-Agriculture
151?
can ripen ours sooner or how we can satisfy the appetite of our people in some other way until our own product gets ready for the market?
Put up a good tariff.

I was just wondering if that was-it. If I were a fruit grower I suppose that would appeal to me a little more than it does now. As a matter of fact there is a substantial tariff on these articles.
I see my hon. friends from over the way pricking up their ears at the suggestion of increasing the duty on fruit; they are the great buyers-the home market, if you like- for the fruit of British Columbia. I frankly admit that I would like to see something done to keep our market for our own fruit, provided that the price to the consumer was not increased.

If my hon. friend would
look a little more in this direction instead of always looking in the direction of my hon. friends to my left, he would probably agree with more of our suggestions.

Oh, I am not getting squint-eyed at all; I am keeping track of both. If my hon. friend has any method to suggest whereby we can keep out other fruits or vegetables without raising the price to the Canadian consumer, I shall be pleased to consider it and perhaps to make a recommendation in regard to it to the Acting Minister of Finance the next time he come3 down with his budget.

The growers of early fruits and vegetables in Canada have suffered a good deal of loss on account of the people to the south of us being able to produce these articles earlier in the year, so that by the time the Canadian fruits and vegetables, strawberries, early potatoes and so on, are ready for the market the palate of the people has been largely satisfied by the imported articles and the farmer does not benefit by the higher prices. These goods that are brought in from the south, grown in Carolina, Florida, California and other places, are sold at very high prices. They are luxuries, because they are out of season, and as it is agreed that it is a good thing to tax luxuries under certain conditions my hon. friend might find in that a means of getting revenue. It is a well known fact that during the tree-planting boom in the western States, particularly in Washington, Oregon and Idaho, a great many areas were over planted, and in their large home market, found in centres of considerable size such as Chicago, Boston, Philadelphia, New York and other places, they are able to dis-97
pose of their best grades of fruit, nicely put up, at high prices, and they are able then to slump off their poorer grades in this country, much to the disadvantage of the Canadian grower. It would seem that until such time as the fruit growing industry of this country is able to get on its feet it requires a little protection. I understand that there is no duty on the citrous fruits, which are also a competitor with locally grown fruits,. May I ask how far the dumping clause has been applied with regard to the importation of these fruits from the American side?

The Minister of Customs (Mr. Bureau) is not here and I would not like to give any information offhand without being sure of it. I understand, however, that the dumping clause has been applied in such cases; it may even be applied to articles that come in free. As to the other question that my hon. friend has raised, it is worthy of perhaps fuller consideration than it has ever been given. I have had an opportunity during the last few years of visiting the orchards of Canada, an opportunity that I had not had before. I had often heard of the Annapolis valley, and it was a real treat to go through that country in harvest time, or in blossom time. I was in Niagara in blossom time, and in British Columbia the year before at harvest time. In endeavouring to find a solution we must remember that a straight duty always puts the price up to the consumer. I may say that in view of the dumping and other conditions in connection with inportation it has been a little more difficult for foreign fruit to get in this last two years, particularly this last year, and we have heard no criticism from the prairies about it. I would not like to see it get to the point where there would be criticism because you are establishing friendly business relations with British Columbia, trading back and forth, and therefore I would look in some other direction for a solution than simply a straight jacking up of the duty, which would only mean a higher price to the consumer.
This suggestion has been made. Let us take 100, for convenience, as representing the tariff. It has been suggested that during the three months when the early fruit and vegetables are coming in, and before ours is on the market, the tariff might be put up to, say, 125, and during the other ten months of the year be put down to 75, making an average of 100. I do not know whether it is workable or not, but it might help to solve the situation. Then the man who felt that he could afford to buy the early fruit and vegetables would

Supply-Agriculture

pay a duty of 125, we will say, and the man who felt that he had to wait for a lower price would get his fruit in on a 75 duty. There is one objection to that, and it is that you are discriminating against the poorer man. Why should he not be able to buy early fruit and vegetables just the same as the wealthy man? That merely shows that there is no perfect solution, and all you can do is to accept a solution that presents the minimum disadvantages and the maximum advantages. I think that solution suggested is worthy of consideration. I do not know whether it is workable or not, because it would involve changing the tariff twice a year. The tariff would be kept up at 125, 'let us say, while the early fruits and vegetables are coming in until perhaps the 1st of July, till ours come on the market, and then drop to 75, when the great mass of the public would buy their fruit and vegetables at the lower rate, and at the same time it would not prohibit those who felt they could afford to buy the early fruit and vegetables at the higher price from doing so. That is only one suggested solution. I do not know whether this discussion is in order, Mr. Chairman. The Department of Agriculture may have views on this subject, but they are not considered authoritative or necessarily expert.

May I help out the
minister? I would throw out the suggestion to him and to the ex-Minister of Agriculture to tell the fruit growers of Canada just what they told the farmers of the prairie provinces, to go into mixed farming. I think that would help them out.
I have been suggesting that, and I think they are going into poultry raising, because you see poultry running in the orchards.

It is a good deal easier to offer advice of that kind than to show the fruit farmer in British Columbia how he is going to adopt it. He has a ten or twenty acre orchard perhaps, bought at high prices, from $250 an acre upwards, and he has to get a high priced crop to begin to pay the interest on his investment. He has to pay high irrigation charges, from $10 an acre upwards, and he has to pay continuous costs, for pruning, spraying and so forth, and on a ten-acre farm there is very little chance of his doing much of a mixed farming business. He does keep a few poultry, as has been said, but I think his situation is certainly deserving of far more serious consideration, and I think a little more sympathy from certain elements

in this Dominion and in this House than it has received. We have in British Columbia something over $40,000,000 invested in the fruit-growing business, and in the last three or four years these men have had a very discouraging path to tread. I do not suppose that last year they got more than half what it cost them to produce their apples. The average price for the crop of last year would be 50 cents a box, and it would cost on the average throughout the fruit-growing sections of British Columbia anywhere from 75 cents to $1 a box to produce that fruit, and it is small encouragement to the man who has his all invested in that business to tell him that he must pull up his trees which he has planted, and which have taken six or seven years to come into fruition and go into mixed farming. Any encouragement that can be given by the Department of Agriculture and by the Minister of Finance towards fostering and keeping alive a business which is engaging the attention of a large portion of the population of British Columbia, and of the very best class of our population, is certainly deserving of the serious consideration of this House.

I anticipated the suggestion from my friend to my left, that we should advise these men to go into mixed farming. I remember going down the Okanagan valley at a time when it was being changed from a cattle-ranging country into a fruit-growing country. Along with me was a very glib talker from Spokane, Washington. We were doing missionary work in connection with farmers' institutes. My business was to speak first at all these meetings. He was more experienced than I was, and I fell for it, and acted as a sort of house warmer for him at all our meetings. I preached chickens, eggs, hogs;, and maxed farming in all its branches to these people, but they would not listen to me. They were all anxious to hear this other man who told them about the ten-acre farm and the big red apple, and the tremendous market for that apple. They could never grow too many. If they could not sell them on the Canadian side, they could sell them on the American side, and even across the water in the Old Country. I remember fifteen years later meeting the same man again at an irrigation convention at Penticton at the lower end of the Okanagan lake, and this time he was preaching to them: "Don't keep all your eggs in one basket; keep a few hogs, keep a cow, keep some chickens, and grow your stuff on the side." "Why," I said, "what is

the matter? You have changed your tune entirely." "Oh," he said, "conditions have changed."
I quite agree with what my bon. friend has said, that if they had gone in for mixed farming and grown fruit on the side they would have been in a safer position than they are in to-day. However, I think that now they are located there, and I feel the minister is anxious to assist them in every possible way, we should try and meet their problems, just as we should try and meet the problems of our friends on the prairies, and the problems of our friends in the Maritime provinces, for we are not going to have a real good Canada until tve have done everything we can to meet the problems of all these people, in an endeavour to unite them and make this one great country.
With regard to fruit growing, there is no question at all that we can produce the very best in the world, and I think perhaps one of the best means of helping out these men is to assist in every way possible with cold storage facilities, and also in the development of our export market. I would ask the minister to give us a little description of the exhibit of fruit which he proposes to have at the big exhibition in London this year.

As a preliminary,
and without making it too long, I might say that an investigation made by members of my staff when they were over there last year goes to show that our fruit stands the highest of any on the British market, our fruit and our storage eggs. Those are the only two things in which we take the top-notch place. Last year again we took the sweepstakes for our fruit at the Manchester Fruit Exhibition. Now, having these victories to our credit we feel more encouraged to put up a good exhibit at the British Empire Exhibition which, of course, will consist of this year's fruit. We are going to put on the very best we can. We have one of the finest collections of grass seeds that has ever been brought together on this continent, and we have the best exhibit of tobacco leaf that the Canadian counties engaged in tobacco growing will produce. We are going to do the same thing for fruit. I cannot give any details until the arrangements are completed, but we shall exhibit apples, and peaches and pears. Of course, great care will have to be taken in the selection of the varieties. I understand the exhibition will last for six months. At any rate it will be open sufficiently long to enable us to get fruit from Canada to London in time.

I think on this occasion when our fruit will be exhibited in competition with fruit from all other parts of the British Empire, we should spare no effort to make the show one of the best we have ever put up.
Either do that or keep away altogether.
Yes.
Who will be in charge of the fruit exhibit?

We have a repre-senative over there, he is really an appointee of the Department of Trade and Commerce. Mr. Forsythe Smith will be one of the gentlemen, and Messrs. Rhodes and Nunnick the other two. A number of hon. gentlemen, including members from British Columbia, have asked the minister to help out the fruit growers in that province. I should like to know from the minister how he is going to do that. We from the prairie provinces have had the experience of paying considerably more than is necessary for British Columbia apples, and more than we pay for apples shipped from the United States. The British Columbia growers also have the privilege of supplying our market without paying any duty. I think the tariff on imported apples is about thirty cents a box. In addition the British Columbia growers have the advantage of better freight rates and still they cannot compete with the American apple. If the minister can devise any other way of helping the British Columbia growers out when they enjoy such an advantageous situation as that I should like to see it outlined.

I have already
mentioned a number of ways in which we are helping them out. We are doing that by means of dehydrating plants, and then we are establishing pre-cooling plants. That is one way of helping rather than boosting the duties. I may say this: Unless one has been very
Supply-Agriculture

closely in touch with the fruit industry he knows very little of what it means to enter a market just hungry for early vegetables and fruits, and then arrive on that market two months later when it is saturated with these products. It is the latter position that we are in. I am not going to bite at the suggestion that we run up the duty, not at all, but I do say that we should do pretty nearly everything else we can think of, because our growers labour under a tremendous disadvantage in regard to early vegetables. I made a suggestion as to an adjustment that might, unless it disturbs the trade or is utterly impracticable, meet the situation without raising the general tariff. It is that the duty should be greater at one time where the wealthy are concerned and lower at another time in the interests of the average man. I may say that there are exhibits outside of Canada which are administered by the Department of Immigration. These are intended to promote immigration and I believe are in charge of Mr. Tolmie, with whom is associated Mr. DeHart. We have a big enterprise under way, but I understand from my deputy that it is not quite ready for announcement yet. It provides for very expensive practical advertising of our dairy products by keeping them before the public. However, I had better not reveal any more with respect to it, otherwise I shall disclose all the details.

What is the estimate for that
advertising scheme?

We hope it will
largely carry itself.
Yes, ten years hence.

We hope the enterprise will largely pay for itself. The scheme is not completed yet. Of course no plan that I know of that the government enters into entirely carries itself. If you are out for education you must expect it to cost you something. There will be little losses here and little losses there, but if the scheme reaches fruition I do not think there will be any cause for complaint. The details are almost complete.
