I received a letterwhich unfortunately I do not have in my hand at present-from Mr. Bums, secretary of the Western Canada Fruit Shippers' Association. He told me in the letter, and I have his per-

mission to mention it, that one of the reasons why the apple growers of British Columbia find themselves in the position they are in to-day is because they are very poor business men. He claims that they have the advantage of a duty of thirty cents a box. He mentioned Edmonton as the point at which they have an advantage of thirty cents a box duty on American apples, and an advantage of 164 cents a box in freight. He told me the reason the apple growers in British Columbia are in such a position is because they hold their apples for a higher price and do not sell them at the right time. He tells me in his letter that they are the poorest business men with whom he ever came in contact.
I desire to tell the hon. member and the members of the House generally that if there is one class of agriculturist or horticulturist, engaged in the cultivation of the soil in Canada-
May I interrupt to say that the statement I made did not originate with me, the words I cited are those of Mr Burns.

I quite understand
But if there is one class in Canada that possesses more than ordinary ability it is the fruit growing class, and especially that in British Columbia. The United Farmers and the wheat growers of the western prairies attribute what little degree of success they may have had to co-operative work among themselves. And I will tell them, and will inform the House, that in the fruit-growing sections of British Columbia there is the finest organization of a co-operative nature for handling fruit that possibly exists in Canada. Last year, which was the first year of their operations, they succeeded in building up without a dollar of capital a four million dollar organization. They have contracts from growers covering about 80 per cent of the fruit growers of the Okanagan, the Salmon river and the Kootenay district. I think this should appeal to hon. members from the prairie, as here is an opportunity for them to assist in the co-operative business for which they stand so firmly. I do not believe the gentleman quoted by the hon. member who last spoke was well informed. I know that some of his statements will certainly not bear investigation. These men are not holding their apples to get a price. From the time the apples are ready to be plucked they are anxious, and they are pushing ahead, to get them into the market. Hon. members will understand that when we went into the fruit

Supply-Agriculture
growing business in British Columbia on a commercial scale the prairie provinces were absorbing two or three hundred thousand immigrants a year, and it looked as though the market would keep ahead of the production, but such has not turned out to be the case. We have had to push forward for markets all over the world. We sent apples to England last year, and for the first shipment we got good prices, but the next shipment was a drug on the market. The fruit from Washington and Oregon arrived at the time ours got into the market, and we got poor prices for most of the fruit sent to Great Britain. We send shipments to New Zealand, South Africa and to Scandinavian countries, and we are continually reaching out all over the world to find markets to absorb the production which is increasing. A great many of the orchards are still far from mature bearing age, and it is becoming an increasingly hard problem every year to know what to do with the production which has increased so rapidly during the past few years. I am sorry that any statement stigmatizing the fruit growers of the Okanagan valley as the poorest business men of the country should be uttered in this House. I think it is a slander upon them, and I am absolutely certain they will compare favourably as to their business ability and agricultural qualifications with any class in Canada.

I quite agree with the
hon. gentleman who has just spoken that from one angle they possibly excel any business organization in Canada. I do not know of any other organization that has made the extreme use they have of the dumping clause. I think in that regard at least they probably excel any organization in Canada. No doubt they are also very adept at making use of our customs tariff and several other things, but I think that their undertakings are wholly on a different line from those of the grain growers. For instance, they go out, without asking any help of that nature, into the markets of the world and try to establish their business.
I would ask the hon. minister to allow this item to stand. I have considerable matter to deal with, and I did not expect it was coming up tonight; therefore I am not prepared to offer my suggestions for the consideration of the committee. I would appreciate it very much if the minister would allow this item to stand till a future sitting of the committee.

We have only
passed one item. I would like very much to get one more through, and I think the committee will give my hon. friend all the latitude he desires on any item, because perhaps he may not be in the House the next time this item is called. Occasionally such a thing-has happened. If he will be good natured and let the item go through, I will be equally good natured and let him present his information on any other item, and I am sure the committee will consent to that. We have had a very interesting and, I hope, useful discussion, but I would like to make some progress.

I think the minister is a
little bit over-anxious. He has done extremely well to get one item through so soon, because we have sometimes spent a day on one item, and in case I might not be here on a future occasion, as the minister has suggested with regard to the hon. member for East Edmonton (Mr. Kellner), I would like to put on Hansard part of a letter which came to me from the Western Canada Fruit Jobbers' Association. The matter has been referred to so often here tonight, that I think this is the proper time to place the matter before the committee. This is in reference to	the luxury tax on fruit. A
resolution was passed at the annual meeting of the Canadian Horticultural Council asking for a luxury tax on fruit. I will read part of the letter, as follows:
If you will investigate the present duty on fruits you will find that apples carry 30 cents per box; sweet potatoes 30 per cent; all vegetables 30 per cent; melons 3 cents each; cantaloupe 3 cents each; peaches 1 cent per pound, weight of package included; plums, apricots and pears i cent per pound; grapefruit $1 per hundred; grapes and all berries 2 cents per pound.
Any luxury tax asked for on fruit shows a lack of intelligence and an impertinence on the part of those making the application. It also demonstrates just how far they might go in asking for protection.
For instance, cantaloupes grown in Ontario are seldom seen in the West, Winnipeg being as far west as they come due to poor carrying quality and lateness of season. This duty was put on to satisfy a few growers in the Niagara peninsula, and the rest of Canada must pay. It is very questionable if there should be any duty on most fruits to-day, especially in western Canada, where none are grown and where the importations are not in competition with the Canadian grown products, either in British Columbia or Ontario.
To demonstrate the absurdity of a luxury tax on all fruits and vegetables, we know that British Columbia could consume all peaches and apricots produced in British Columbia as well as pears. The coast jobbers sold in 1922, 34,222 boxes of pears; 104,501 boxes of peaches and 55,823 crates of apricots, and it was necessary to import some from the United States for their market, so this alone clearly indicates the senselessness of any application for a luxury tax.
We venture to say that nine-tenths of the fruit and vegetables sold in western Canada, outside of apples, must be imported, if we are going to keep the people supplied.
The luxury tax is only increasing the burden on the consumers. Bartlett pears last for two months, while we only have the British Columbia product for 10 days

Supply-Agriculture
and at the most, three weeks. Apricots from British Columbia were not available for more than a week last year. Vancouver ordered 10 cars of peaches last season and could only get delivery of five. British Columbia Granvenstein apple circular No. 4, of August 4th, 1923, from Associated Growers, Vernon, stated they had not sufficient to make straight cars. Their plum circular of August 3rd, 1923, stated "Not enough for mixed cars".
As shown above there is not the slightest justification for a further tax or duty on fruits or vegetables.
We have a letter from the Customs and Excise Department, Ottawa, stating that whenever the selling price of goods from United States, to the purchaser in Canada is more than 5 per cent below the fair market value of the goods for home consumption the import is subject to the dumping duty.
The fair market value, this year, for home consumption in the United States as set by the growers in British Columbia on C. grade apples, was $1.10 and the jobbers were assessed 15 per cent on $1.10 because the apples purchased in the United States were purchased at a price which was more than 15 per cent below $1.10.
If it can be proven that the United States growers are selling for export to Canada at a lower price than for home consumption, then probably our industry should be protected, but in the case of apples we could buy good apples at Washington for 80 cents, which was the price sold anyone in the United States. Why pay dumping duty because the British Columbia growers claim the growers in the United States should be getting $1.10?
In Washington the cost of packing a box of apples is figured out at 42 cents, everything included; while in British Columbia they figure their cost up to nearly 80 cents.
The duty on apples was increased in 1916 from 10 cents to 30 cents per box. The reason given was on account of the war and insufficient help in British Columbia to take care of the crop. Is there any justification for this duty remaining on now? We are of the opinion that this 30 cents per box duty and lower freights to some points, is more than sufficient protection for the Canadian grower.
The farmers on the prairies have been called upon to pay some 65 cents per box more than they should and more than the farmer in the neighbouring States, for his apples.
The imposition of the dumping duty means we are trading in the dark not knowing just exactly what our costs are until after the goods are received and reshipped out, the duty in some cases being applied after we have even made collection.
Surely the present duties are sufficient, in view of conditions under which we are struggling at present. The Canadian producer can develop conditions sufficiently to stand up against outside competition if he wishes to.
We wish, as jobbers, to make application to have the Dumping Act amended or customs collectors notified not to impose dumping duty on fruits and vegetables entering Canada and pray that our request receive immediate and favourable consideration.
I am just afraid, because of the wavering attitude which the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) seems to take when he approaches the question of helping out the British Columbia fruit men, that he may be considering the imposition of a luxury tax on fruit, and it seems to me that the wholesale jobbers of fruit have in this letter made out a splendid case against any such tax as that. Further, I think they have made out a good case for the removal of the present 
dumping act as far as it applies to fruit. I think it is an outrageous law that the Minister of Customs and Excise (Mr. Bureau) can, of his own volition, set the price which he considers it costs the United States' grower to raise apples. I do not think he knows nearly as much about that question as the United States' growers themselves. Surely when there is a protection of 30 cents a box and an advantage in the freight rate, that should be sufficient protection for the fruit men in British Columbia. I am glad to hear that the growers in British Columbia are getting together; that they have such a splendid co-operative association, and if their industry can be saved, surely through this cooperative selling association, with a protection of 30 cents a box and an advantage in the freight rate, they do not need to come to this parliament and ask for anything more in the shape of a luxury tax or a dumping duty.

I have been very much interested in this discussion in connection with fruit in Canada and this matter, of protecting the fruit growers on the Pacific coast. It was my privilege last summer to visit the Okanagan valley and to make some observations in the western cities in the Okanagan valley as well as in Seattle and Spokane. I was pleased to see the beautiful fruit, because I was there at the time that the apples were ripe. I was much interested in fruit growing in the Okanagan valley and on the Pacific coast. I think a good deal of credit is due to the British Columbia men for the manner in which they ship their fruit. They deserve a good deal more credit than the Ontario fruit growers for the manner in which they have conducted their business
11 p.m. and the way in which they have presented their goods for sale. They have a very favourable climate. Their land is not more expensive than land in the state of Washington. I visited my brother in Washington who has a fruit farm near Spokane. He had an apple orchard of the most beautiful trees that I have ever cast eyes on, and he was so discouraged with it that he was thinking of cutting it. down, because there was no profit in it. He was growing fruit on that land that was estimated to be worth $250 an acre; it costs $12 an acre to irrigate it, and he had to ship the fruit to Canada at some distance over the railways. If he could do that under those conditions and undersell fruit growers in British Columbia, there is something the matter. I do not

Supply-Agriculture
see why the British Columbia men cannot compete with men in the state of Washington in marketing their fruit on the prairie provinces. When I came to Edmonton, I noticed that they had Ontario plums in that city. That surprised me because an acquaintance of mine in Ontario a couple of years ago could not pick his plums and ship them about one hundred miles west, and they were allowed to rot in the orchard. I made inquiries in a store as to where the plums came from and I was told that they came from Ontario. I was somewhat surprised because I knew that in eastern Ontario fruit growers in many cases were not able to market their plums at all and they did not intend to pick them because they could not get the freight and the price of the baskets.
I am opposed to the principle of protection to fruit farmers just as much as I am opposed to the principle of protection to men engaged in mixed farming or any other kind of farming. If we Canadians cannot follow any branch of farming in a certain district, we had better go somewhere else where we can compete with the world. I claim that we farmers in Canada are able to compete with the world without any protection whatever; but we want to be able to buy in the cheapest market if we are to compete in the cheapest market of the world. Therefore, the prairie farmers ought to be able to buy in the cheapest market, and the British Columbia fruit men ought to be able to sell them their fruit. While our eastern men are not producing as beautiful an apple as the men on the Pacific coast, they are able to sell their apples in Great Britain. I noticed in one of the reports which I picked up that Nova Scotia had shipped in the neighbourhood of a million barrels or over. I know that Ontario fruit growers, if they cannot ship West, can ship to the Old Country, and in sections of Ontario where we do not profess to produce the best apples in Canada, we can ship either east or west without any protection whatever. Surely, the men with that favourable climate on the Pacific coast can compete with fruit growers in the state of Washington without any protection. We have in western Ontario men who are seeking protection also, men who belong to that element of manufacturers who need protection in order that they may exist in that most fertile section of the Dominion of Canada on the Niagara peninsula. I have not much faith in those men who must have protection in order to carry on their business. I think the remark was rather jocular when the suggestion was made that the fruit men should go into mixed farming. By the way let me say that when I was in Spokane, without any joking about the matter, my brother was seriously thinking of starting a herd of Holstein cows in connection with his farm of ten acres. His idea was that fertilizer was getting so hard to obtain for his orchard that he could keep cows profitably-and I believe he could-and make as much money out of his cows as out of his fruit. I believe that is quite possible.
As regards the fruit in Ontario and the home market, I have wondered where the fruit men are going to get that market. We have heard a lot of talk recently about a home market. Where are we going to get it and how ? The manufacturers are not able to make up their end of the market for the fruit growers and the farmers are failing to make a market for the manufacturers. Where are they going to get the home market, with one dependent on the other for a market and nobody having it? That is the situation exactly. I cannot understand the reasoning of some hon. gentlemen. I have been sitting patiently listening for a solution to this home market question. My opinion is that the farmers of Canada, the men of experience in Canada, who have been producing stuff for the market, cannot see that it is anything but a joke when people talk about a home market.
I picked up to-day a report sent me by one of the departments at Washington stating that after one hundred years in the United States-and that country, we are told in this House, is far in advance of us-the manufacturers are not yet able, notwithstanding all the immigration there, to provide a home market for the agricultural products of the farmers. Now, if we have to wait one hundred years in this country before we can get a home market for the produce of our farms, I am afraid our farmers will be pretty badly off. To-day we are exporting fruit and all sorts of farm products to the markets of the world and we are not afraid to compete in those markets with producers anywhere. We are bound to compete with outsiders in butter, cheese, beef, wheat and everything else we produce, and there is no use talking about providing a home market; for as I have just stated, if after a hundred years of manufacturing activity in the United States the farmers there are still unable to find an adequate home market, the prospect is very poor indeed for the Canadian farmer. I claim that we are in a position to compete with the rest of the world, and we are going to do so. It was pointed out in the budget debate last night that we were sending a great deal of money to the United States. Surely if we are selling so many million dollars' worth of our products abroad we can afford
Supply-Agriculture

to buy a few million from other countries.
Talking about fruit, I might observe that the people in the Niagara peninsula have been giving the manufacturers in Toronto the benefit of the most wonderful dumping clause we have ever seen. Gentlemen from the West may laugh at the business ability of the men on the Pacific coast, but I think they are in advance of the people in the Niagara district, and they are dumping their fruit on the Toronto market when they cannot get the cost of their containers or pay their freight. Owing to circumstances that the fruit growers cannot control, this fruit is being dumped on the market in Toronto at less than cost, and that suits the consumer of fruit in Toronto quite well. Now, I happened to be raised in a garden myself-I was brought up in an orchard, so to speak-and I may tell hon. gentlemen that as a practical farmer I refuse to grow anything unless I can depend upon being able to ship my produce to the markets of the world. I find that the men who do that are the successful farmers in Ontario. If you produce cattle, wheat, cheese, butter or bacon, you have a ready market and cash at all times in the world markets; but if you are content to cater to the home market you have nothing stable to depend upon. Some of the city men of Toronto bought a farm in the fruit section not long ago and they thought that they would reap a great profit from it. I was acquainted with them, but they would not listen to any advice I had to offer, because some of the gentlemen of Toronto are like that. At any rate they bought this farm for 140,000 and started growing fruit on it. It is a rather long story to tell, but out of a total of the first crop of peaches, 25,000 baskets, they marketed 15,000, while 10,000 baskets rotted in the orchards, and so far as the apples were concerned they were unable to pick them. So that the profit which they anticipated proved in the long run to be a considerable loss. We are getting away from that kind of business in our part of the country and are producing stuff that we can sell in the markets of the world. Our people are making a fair success of that method and are certainly doing better than they would if they catered to the home market. The fact is that the home market is governed by the little surplus which we are able to sell. Some people contend that 80 per cent of our farm produce is consumed at home; this would leave 20 per cent to ship abroad which fixes the price for all. I have no patience with 
those who would grant protection to the fruit men of Niagara or of the Pacific coast, any more than I have with granting protection to the manufacturers of the city of Toronto.
